phrases.translation: Ṭâ-Sĩn-Mĩm
phrases.explanation: The chapter opens with three letters standing alone. The commentary refers back to what it has already set out about the disconnected letters that open several chapters, and records two reports about this one, that it is an oath sworn by Allah and belongs to His names, and that it is a name among the names of the Quran. No meaning is built on it here. The letters stand at the threshold of the chapter as a signal of a book unlike speech.

phrases.translation: These are the verses of the clear Book
phrases.explanation: The verse names what follows. These are the verses of the clear Book, and the commentary explains the clarity as the quality by which anyone who reflects on the text with understanding sees that it comes from Allah, and that Muhammad did not invent it but received it from his Lord. The book is called clear because it clears up its own origin. The argument of the chapter begins with the book itself rather than with its hearers.

phrases.translation: Perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ will grieve yourself to death
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to the messenger's grief. Perhaps you will grieve yourself to death, and the commentary explains the rare verb as destroying and ruining oneself, with one report describing a man driving his soul out of his body out of longing for his people's belief. The concern is not for his own safety but for their refusal. The verse names a sorrow so heavy that it is pictured as self destruction.

phrases.translation: over their disbelief
phrases.explanation: The cause of that sorrow is stated. It is over their disbelief, and the commentary adds that the grief came from wanting them to believe and seeing that they would not. The messenger is not rebuked for caring but is shown how much he cares. The chapter opens by acknowledging the weight of a mission among people who do not respond.

phrases.translation: If We willed, We could send down upon them a ˹compelling˺ sign from the heavens,
phrases.explanation: The verse offers a different way the matter could have been settled. If We willed, We could send down upon them a sign from the heavens, and the commentary explains that such a sign would have subdued them at once, so that not one of them would commit a disobedient act afterwards. The possibility is stated to show that their belief was not prevented by any lack of power. What was withheld was compulsion, not proof.

phrases.translation: leaving their necks bent in ˹utter˺ submission to it
phrases.explanation: The effect of such a sign is then pictured. Their necks would be left bent in submission to it, and the commentary explains the posture as the bowing of people humbled by what they had seen. It records the view of some that the necks here mean the leaders and nobles of the people, subdued before the sign. Either way the image is of a submission produced by force rather than by conviction, which is why it was not sent.

phrases.translation: Whatever new reminder comes to them from the Most Compassionate,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes the actual response. Whatever new reminder comes to them from the Most Compassionate, and the commentary explains the reminder as what Allah reveals to the Prophet so that he may bring it to their memory, including the proofs of his truthfulness. The word new suggests a fresh arrival each time, not a single message heard once. The title Most Compassionate is used even as they refuse.

phrases.translation: they always turn away from it
phrases.explanation: The refusal is stated flatly. They always turn away from it, and the commentary explains this as turning from listening and neglecting to direct their understanding toward what was said. The fault is not that the reminder failed to reach them but that they would not attend to it. The verse describes a habit rather than a single incident, which is why the next verse speaks of a consequence still coming.

phrases.translation: They have certainly denied ˹the truth˺,
phrases.explanation: The verse states the verdict. They have certainly denied the truth, and the commentary explains the denial as their rejection of the reminder that came from Allah and their turning their backs on it. Denial is named as a settled fact rather than a suspicion. Everything that follows in the chapter about the nations of the past rests on this verdict, since the same refusal has appeared before.

phrases.translation: so they will soon face the consequences of their ridicule
phrases.explanation: The consequence is then announced. They will soon face the consequences of their ridicule, and the commentary explains this as the news reaching them of the very matter they mocked, a warning that punishment will descend on them for persisting in disbelief. What they treated as a joke will return as information they cannot dismiss. The verse leaves the timing open and the certainty closed.

phrases.translation: Have they failed to look at the earth,
phrases.explanation: The verse directs them to something they could see. Have they failed to look at the earth, and the commentary explains the question as addressed to those who deny the resurrection and the raising of the dead. The earth lies under their feet and needs no messenger to be examined. The argument begins with observation rather than with scripture, which suits people who have rejected the scripture they were given.

phrases.translation: ˹to see˺ how many types of fine plants We have caused to grow in it
phrases.explanation: What they would see is then named. How many types of fine plants We have caused to grow in it, and the commentary explains the noble pair as beautiful growth, with one report describing it as the vegetation from which people and livestock eat. The word pair suggests kinds and varieties rather than a single crop. Land that was dead now carries abundance, which is the comparison the next verse will draw.

phrases.translation: Surely in this is a sign.
phrases.explanation: The verse draws the conclusion. Surely in this is a sign, and the commentary explains the sign as a proof for those who deny the resurrection, since the power that made the barren earth produce cannot be unable to raise the dead from their graves. The argument is from the lesser to the greater, and both are works of the same hand. What grows every season is evidence for what has not yet happened.

phrases.translation: Yet most of them would not believe
phrases.explanation: The verse then states the sad qualification. Yet most of them would not believe, and the commentary explains that this was already established in Allah's knowledge and that most of them would not accept what the Prophet brought. The sign is not lacking in clarity but in recipients willing to receive it. The verse prepares the refrain that returns throughout the chapter after each destroyed people.

phrases.translation: And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The verse names the two qualities that frame the whole chapter. Your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful, and the commentary explains the first as power in retribution from which no one who is punished can escape, and the second as mercy toward whoever turns back from disbelief, so that his past is not held against him. The pair is held together rather than divided. The chapter repeats it after each destroyed people, so that judgement and mercy are not seen apart.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when your Lord called out to Moses,
phrases.explanation: The verse begins the first of the long narratives. Remember when your Lord called out to Moses, and the commentary explains this as Allah addressing Moses son of Imran and sending him to a wrongdoing people, meaning the unbelievers of Pharaoh's court. The call is described as a calling out, which gives the scene a voice and a moment. The chapter turns from the Meccans to an older confrontation so that the pattern may be recognised.

phrases.translation: “Go to the wrongdoing people—
phrases.explanation: The command itself is quoted. Go to the wrongdoing people, and the commentary notes that the phrase is completed by the next verse, which names them as the people of Pharaoh. The task begins with a journey and a destination rather than with a doctrine. Moses is sent into the strongest court of his age, which makes the Meccan opposition look small by comparison and the outcome of that errand worth remembering.

phrases.translation: the people of Pharaoh.
phrases.explanation: The verse names the destination. The people of Pharaoh, and the commentary explains that this phrase specifies the wrongdoing people named in the previous verse and identifies them as the unbelieving court of Egypt. The name is given before anything else about them, because everything depends on who they were and what power they held. The reader is meant to feel the weight of the errand.

phrases.translation: Will they not fear ˹Allah˺?”
phrases.explanation: The question that follows shapes the message. Will they not fear Allah, and the commentary explains this as asking whether they will not fear His punishment for their disbelief, with the words so say to them understood from the context. The question is a first approach rather than a final warning. Moses is not told to demand obedience at once but to appeal to the fear that might still be in them.

phrases.translation: He replied, “My Lord! I fear
phrases.explanation: The verse begins Moses' answer. He replied, My Lord, I fear, and the commentary explains the fear as his apprehension about the people of Pharaoh to whom he had been commanded to go. The reply is not a refusal of the command but a description of the difficulty in carrying it. A messenger who admits his fear is more credible than one who pretends to none, and the verse lets him speak before Allah answers him.

phrases.translation: that they will reject me
phrases.explanation: What he fears is then named. That they will reject me, and the commentary explains the rejection as their denial of what he would say, that Allah had sent him to them. The fear is about the reception of the message rather than about his own safety, which the following verses show he also weighs. The verse opens a dialogue between a prophet and his Lord that the chapter will use to steady its own messenger.

phrases.translation: And ˹so˺ my heart will be broken and my tongue will be tied.
phrases.explanation: He states two effects of that rejection. My heart will be broken and my tongue will be tied, and the commentary explains the first as his breast being constricted by their denial, and the second as a difficulty of speech caused by the affliction that had struck his tongue. The two are linked, since grief crowds out speech. He is describing what happens inside him when the message is refused, not what will happen to the message.

phrases.translation: So send Aaron along ˹as a messenger˺
phrases.explanation: The request follows from the difficulty. So send Aaron along as a messenger, and the commentary explains that he asked for his brother, and that the sense is send him to help and support me, though the words that would say this were left out because the meaning was clear. The request is for a companion in speech, not for a replacement. The verse shows a prophet asking for help rather than pretending to need none.

phrases.translation: Also, they have a charge against me,
phrases.explanation: A second danger is added. Also, they have a charge against me, and the commentary explains the charge as the killing he had committed among them, which reports describe as a manslaughter he had been involved in before his flight. The word is the language of a case rather than of a private quarrel. He is being asked to return to people who held a claim against his life.

phrases.translation: so I fear they may kill me.”
phrases.explanation: The consequence of that charge is then stated. So I fear they may kill me, and the commentary explains the fear as his expectation that they would kill him in retaliation for the person he had killed among them. The verse adds a legal fear to the fear of rejection. The two together make his reluctance entirely reasonable, and the answer that comes next addresses both at once.

phrases.translation: Allah responded, “Certainly not! So go, both of you, with Our signs.
phrases.explanation: The answer opens with a flat denial of his fear. Certainly not, Allah responded, and the commentary explains this as a promise that the people of Pharaoh would never kill him. Then comes the command to go with the signs and proofs given to them, with the plural addressing both brothers. The reassurance is not that the way would be easy but that the outcome he dreaded was ruled out.

phrases.translation: We will be with you, listening
phrases.explanation: The verse adds the ground of that confidence. We will be with you, listening, and the commentary explains the listening as Allah hearing what the people of Pharaoh would say to them and how they would answer. The presence is described in terms of attention rather than of power, which is what a speaker needs. The two brothers are sent into a hostile court knowing that every word will be heard.

phrases.translation: Go to Pharaoh and say,
phrases.explanation: The command is repeated with the destination named. Go to Pharaoh and say, and the commentary notes that this is the same errand now given to both brothers together. Nothing has been added to the message and nothing about the danger has been repeated. The second instruction fixes the audience, since the mission was not to Egypt in general but to its ruler.

phrases.translation: ‘We are messengers from the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The words to be spoken are then supplied. We are messengers from the Lord of all worlds, and the commentary notes that the singular word for messenger is used though two are sent, because what is meant is the message itself, which is one. The two men are bringing a single commission from the one Lord of everything. The claim is enormous and is stated in a single sentence.

phrases.translation: ˹commanded to say:˺
phrases.explanation: The verse opens with a parenthetical note. Commanded to say, it reads, marking the words that follow as part of the message the brothers were to deliver. The note separates the content of the demand from the narrative around it. What comes next is therefore not Moses speaking for himself but the point of the whole embassy.

phrases.translation: ‘Let the Children of Israel go with us.’’”
phrases.explanation: The demand is then stated. Let the Children of Israel go with us, and the commentary explains this as the purpose of the mission, that Pharaoh should release the people Israel had been held by. The request is political and concrete rather than abstract. Moses was not sent to argue about theology with a king so much as to take a people out of his hand, which is why the conflict was never going to be settled by discussion.

phrases.translation: Pharaoh protested, “Did we not raise you among us as a child,
phrases.explanation: The verse begins Pharaoh's reply with an old debt. He protests, did we not raise you among us as a child, and the commentary notes that something has been omitted before this, namely that they came and delivered their message and then he answered. He is not responding to the claim about the Lord of all worlds but to the man standing in front of him. The first move is to make Moses small.

phrases.translation: and you stayed several years of your life in our care
phrases.explanation: The second half completes the reproach. You stayed several years of your life in our care, and the commentary explains this as the years he spent among them before he killed the man of the Copts and fled. The argument uses kindness as a claim of ownership. Pharaoh is saying that a man raised at his expense has no standing to come back as a messenger, and the charge is more personal than doctrinal.

phrases.translation: Then you did what you did,
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh names the deed without naming it. Then you did what you did, and the commentary explains the reference as the killing of the man from among the Copts, described in a way that keeps the act in view while avoiding the details. The vague phrasing is a form of pressure, since it makes Moses supply the memory himself. The charge is placed beside the reminder of the upbringing, so that kindness and accusation arrive together.

phrases.translation: being ˹utterly˺ ungrateful!”
phrases.explanation: The accusation ends with a word about gratitude. Being utterly ungrateful, he says, and the commentary records two explanations of the word, that Moses was then among those who disbelieved in Allah according to the religion of Egypt, and that he was among those who rejected the beneficence shown to him. Both readings turn the past into a debt. Pharaoh's case is that a man who was raised and spared has no right to return with a claim.

phrases.translation: Moses replied, “I did it then, lacking guidance
phrases.explanation: Moses answers the charge by admitting the act and naming its quality. I did it then, lacking guidance, and the commentary explains that he acknowledges killing the man and describes himself at that time as one of those who erred, meaning ignorant, before any revelation had come to him forbidding the act. The admission is complete and the excuse is precise. He does not deny the deed but places it before his prophethood rather than within it.

phrases.translation: So I fled from you when I feared you.
phrases.explanation: He then explains why he left. So I fled from you when I feared you, and the commentary explains the flight as his departure from the chiefs of Pharaoh's people for fear that they would kill him over the man he had slain. The fear is stated without shame, in the same way he had stated it to his Lord earlier. The verse traces the road from that flight to his standing in the court, so that his return is not a coincidence.

phrases.translation: Then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers
phrases.explanation: The second half describes what happened in between. Then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers, and the commentary explains the wisdom here as prophethood, and the sending as his being included among those sent to Allah's creation with His message. The two gifts are placed after the flight, not before it. What Pharaoh treats as a criminal returning is a prophet arriving with a commission, and the verse lets Moses say so in the king's own hall.

phrases.translation: How can that be a ‘favour,’ of which you remind me,
phrases.explanation: Moses then takes up the claim of favour. How can that be a favour of which you remind me, he asks, and the commentary explains the point as the upbringing Pharaoh had given him. The question does not deny the kindness but questions what it is worth as an argument. A benefit given to one man is being weighed against a wrong done to a whole people, and the verse sets the two on the same scale.

phrases.translation: when ˹it was only because˺ you ˹have˺ enslaved the Children of Israel?”
phrases.explanation: The reason follows. When it was only because you have enslaved the Children of Israel, and the commentary explains the sense as the favour consisting of raising him while enslaving the rest of his people, with the words and leaving me understood from the context. The kindness was the exception, and the slavery was the rule. Moses turns the charge of ingratitude around by showing what the favour depended on.

phrases.translation: Pharaoh asked, “And what is ‘the Lord of all worlds’?”
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh ignores the argument and asks a question of his own. And what is the Lord of all worlds, he says, and the commentary treats the question as a request for a definition of the one the brothers have named. He does not engage with the enslavement or the charge of ingratitude. The question looks like enquiry but functions as a way of moving the ground of the discussion, since a king who claims divinity has no category for a Lord above him.

phrases.translation: Moses replied, “˹He is˺ the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between,
phrases.explanation: Moses answers with the widest frame available. He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, and the commentary explains this as the owner of both and of all that lies between them. The answer is not a name but a domain, since the question was about authority. Pharaoh rules a strip of land beside a river, and the reply places that strip inside a larger ownership.

phrases.translation: if only you had sure faith.”
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with a condition. If only you had sure faith, and the commentary explains this as saying that if they know with certainty what they perceive, they should be equally certain that their Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. The argument is from ordinary certainty to a conclusion they were resisting. The verse does not threaten here but appeals to the confidence they already placed in the world before their eyes.

phrases.translation: Pharaoh said to those around him, “Did you hear ˹what he said˺?”
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh turns to his court instead of answering. Did you hear what he said, he asks those around him, and the commentary explains that he was addressing the nobles of his people about the words Moses had spoken. The question is not a request for information but a way of drawing in the court. Having no answer to the claim about the Lord of the heavens and the earth, he makes the saying the scandal, so the room hears an outrage rather than an argument.

phrases.translation: Moses added, “˹He is˺ your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers.”
phrases.explanation: Moses continues without waiting to be answered. He is your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, and the commentary explains this as a statement that the One he calls them to worship is the creator of them and of the kings and ancestors before them. The claim moves from the cosmos to their own genealogy. Their fathers, whom they honoured, were made by the same Lord they were being asked to accept, which includes the kings whose memory Egypt revered.

phrases.translation: Pharaoh said ˹mockingly˺,
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh answers with an insult rather than a reply. He speaks mockingly, and the commentary explains that he accused Moses of madness because what Moses said had no meaning for him or for his people. The mockery is not a light remark but a public strategy. A claim that cannot be answered can still be dismissed, and the king chooses to dismiss it by attacking the speaker rather than the speech.

phrases.translation: “Your messenger, who has been sent to you, must be insane.”
phrases.explanation: The charge is then put in words. Your messenger, who has been sent to you, must be insane, and the commentary explains that Pharaoh said this because he and his court were convinced that there was no lord to be worshipped except himself, and that what Moses called them to had no reality behind it. Since they could not conceive of what he described, they concluded that his mind was disordered. The measure of a claim is taken from what the hearers already believe.

phrases.translation: Moses responded: “˹He is˺ the Lord of the east and west, and everything in between,
phrases.explanation: Moses answers with another description of the same Lord. He is the Lord of the east and west, and everything in between, and the commentary explains this as the owner and ruler over the rising of the sun and its setting and all that lies between, not the kings of Egypt who have passed away nor Pharaoh who now rules it. The argument is aimed at a king whose authority ended at the desert's edge. The sun rises outside his borders under another's command.

phrases.translation: if only you had any sense.”
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with a challenge to think. If only you had any sense, and the commentary explains this as saying, if you have understanding by which you grasp what is said to you and what is shown to you. The word is not an insult but a summons to use the reason they already trusted. Once the manifest truth had been put before them, the only remaining defence was to refuse to think.

phrases.translation: Pharaoh threatened, “If you take any other god besides me,
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh abandons argument for threat. If you take any other god besides me, he says, and the commentary explains the word as acknowledging any object of worship other than himself. The claim is now explicit and it is a claim of divinity rather than of kingship. What began as a dispute about freeing a people has become a contest over who may be worshipped, and the king has stated the stake in his own terms.

phrases.translation: I will certainly have you imprisoned.”
phrases.explanation: The punishment is named. I will certainly have you imprisoned, and the commentary explains this as a promise to put him in prison along with those already held there. The threat is not death but confinement, which is enough to end a mission and silence a voice. The verse shows the point at which a regime stops debating and starts using its power, and it is the moment when the signs become necessary.

phrases.translation: Moses responded, “Even if I bring you a clear proof?”
phrases.explanation: Moses answers with a question rather than a retreat. Even if I bring you a clear proof, he asks, and the commentary explains the proof as something demonstrating the truth of what he said. It also explains why he spoke this way, since it is the custom of people to grow calm when treated fairly and to accept the truth once it has been shown. He appeals to the standard Pharaoh would claim to follow, and the appeal leaves the next move with the king.

phrases.translation: Pharaoh demanded, “Bring it then,
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh takes up the offer. Bring it then, he says, and the commentary explains that he was now willing to see the proof, since Moses had asked whether he would be imprisoned even with a clear sign. The demand is a concession and a trap at once, because it accepts a test whose result will bind the one who asked for it. The king believes he can afford to be generous because he cannot imagine losing.

phrases.translation: if what you say is true.”
phrases.explanation: The condition is then added. If what you say is true, and the commentary explains this as saying, if you are truthful in what you convey. The challenge is framed as a matter of honesty rather than power, which places the coming sign on the ground Moses chose. The verse closes the first movement of the narrative with the court waiting to see whether the claim can be backed, and the signs that follow answer the question in a way nobody expected.

phrases.translation: So he threw down his staff and—behold!—it became a real snake
phrases.explanation: The proof begins with a gesture. Moses threw down his staff and behold, it became a real snake, and the commentary explains the word as a male serpent and the description as one that made its serpent form plainly visible to Pharaoh and the nobles of his people. Nothing is said about how the change happened, only that it was seen. A piece of wood becomes a living animal in front of the court that had just called its owner mad.

phrases.translation: Then he drew his hand ˹out of his collar˺
phrases.explanation: A second sign follows the first. Moses drew his hand out of his collar, and the commentary explains that he drew it from the opening of his garment. The gesture is small and the setting is public. The verse notes the movement because the wonder is attached to the man rather than to an object he carries. The same hand that held the staff is now shown empty, which prevents the court from saying that the first wonder was in the rod.

phrases.translation: and it was ˹shining˺ white for all to see
phrases.explanation: The result of that gesture is described. It was shining white for all to see, and the commentary explains this as his hand appearing white and radiant to everyone who looked at it. The phrase for all to see matters in a court that would later claim the signs were illusions. A wonder witnessed by a crowd cannot be dismissed as a private imagining. The two signs together answer the demand Pharaoh made in the previous verses.

phrases.translation: Pharaoh said to the chiefs around him,
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh speaks to his own people first. He said to the chiefs around him, and the commentary explains that these were the nobles of his people gathered in the hall. He does not address Moses at all, which is itself a decision about how the event will be handled. The man who asked for a clear proof now refuses to discuss it with the one who brought it.

phrases.translation: “He is indeed a skilled magician
phrases.explanation: His verdict is then given. He is indeed a skilled magician, and the commentary explains that Pharaoh claimed Moses had bewitched his staff so that it appeared as a serpent, and that he was learned and skilled in sorcery. The explanation keeps the event and removes its meaning. Having seen something beyond his power, the king classifies it as a technique, so that the sign becomes a trick performed by a rival expert.

phrases.translation: who seeks to drive you from your land by his magic.
phrases.explanation: The accusation is given a motive. Who seeks to drive you from your land by his magic, and the commentary explains that Pharaoh was addressing the Coptic nobles while meaning that Moses wanted to take the Children of Israel, their servants, out of Egypt toward Syria. The claim turns a demand for freedom into a threat against the audience. Those listening are told that the man before them intends to take away the labour they profit from.

phrases.translation: So what do you propose?”
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with a question to the court. So what do you propose, Pharaoh asks, and the commentary explains this as asking what they command concerning the matter of Moses and what they advise. A king who has just been shown a sign now hands the decision to his advisers. The question is a way of sharing responsibility for what will be done next, and it sets up the plan of the magicians that follows.

phrases.translation: They replied, “Let him and his brother wait
phrases.explanation: The chiefs answer with a strategy rather than a refutation. They say, let him and his brother wait, and the commentary explains this as a counsel to put Moses and Aaron off and grant them a respite. Delay is chosen because no one in the hall can answer the signs. The proposal also buys time to gather the best opposition available, which means the court has decided to meet a wonder with a bigger performance.

phrases.translation: and dispatch mobilizers to all cities
phrases.explanation: The second half of the advice is practical. Dispatch mobilizers to all cities, and the commentary explains these as men sent into the provinces of Egypt to summon the sorcerers. The kingdom is being organised around a contest. What Pharaoh could not settle by authority he will attempt to settle by spectacle, and the cities of Egypt are put to work finding performers who can match what the court has seen.

phrases.translation: to bring you every skilled magician.”
phrases.explanation: The verse completes the plan. To bring you every skilled magician, and the commentary explains this as summoning all those practiced in sorcery to be gathered before Pharaoh. The word for skilled repeats the word Pharaoh used of Moses, which shows exactly what the court thinks it is dealing with. If Moses is a learned magician, the answer is more learned magicians, and the question of who sent him is left entirely untouched.

phrases.translation: So the magicians were assembled at the set time
phrases.explanation: The plan is carried out. So the magicians were assembled, and the commentary explains that the gatherers Pharaoh had sent brought them together at the time he had fixed with Moses. The machinery of a state is now set in motion over a staff and a hand. The verse marks the point where a private dispute becomes a public event that the whole city will watch.

phrases.translation: on the appointed day
phrases.explanation: The time is then specified. At the set time on the appointed day, and the commentary explains this as the day Pharaoh fixed for the meeting, described elsewhere as the day of the festival when the people would be gathered in the forenoon. The choice of a festival guarantees an audience. What began in a palace hall will now be settled in front of a crowd, which raises the stakes for both sides.

phrases.translation: And the people were asked, “Will you join the gathering
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to the crowd. The people were asked whether they would join the gathering, and the commentary explains the question as an invitation to watch what the two sides would do and to see to whom the victory would fall, Moses or the sorcerers. A contest between a prophet and hired performers has been turned into public entertainment. The court wants witnesses, and the verse shows how a matter of truth can be staged as a spectacle for a crowd.

phrases.translation: so that we may follow the magicians if they prevail?”
phrases.explanation: The crowd is given a reason to attend. So that we may follow the magicians if they prevail, and the commentary explains that the word rendered perhaps carries the sense of so that, since these were people of Pharaoh's religion and could only want the outcome that confirmed it. They were not coming to judge between two claims but to see their own side win. The verse shows a crowd already decided, which is why the sign that follows must be unmistakable rather than persuasive.

phrases.translation: When the magicians came, they asked Pharaoh,
phrases.explanation: The magicians arrive and open with business. When they came, they asked Pharaoh, and the commentary explains that they came to the appointment with Moses and the gathering Pharaoh had fixed. Before the contest begins, the terms are settled. They are professionals hired for an occasion, and they treat the confrontation as work to be paid for. The verse keeps their request in view so that the reader sees what they thought was at stake.

phrases.translation: “Shall we have a ˹suitable˺ reward if we prevail?”
phrases.explanation: The question is then quoted. Shall we have a suitable reward if we prevail, and the commentary explains that they were asking for payment for the magic they would perform if they defeated Moses. The word reward carries the sense of a wage. They have no interest in who is right, only in who wins and what winning pays, which is exactly the difference between them and the man who threw down a staff without asking for anything.

phrases.translation: He replied, “Yes, and you will then certainly be among those closest to me.”
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh answers with a promise that grows as it is spoken. Yes, he says, and you will then certainly be among those closest to me, and the commentary explains this as a promise of the reward and of nearness to the king. He offers status as well as money, which is the currency of a court. The verse shows how a ruler recruits loyalty when he cannot command belief, and what the magicians are bought with: not truth but nearness to power.

phrases.translation: Moses said to them, “Cast whatever you wish to cast.”
phrases.explanation: Moses answers with a permission. Cast whatever you wish to cast, he says, and the commentary explains this as an invitation to throw down their ropes and staffs. He gives away the first move and the appearance of initiative. A man relying on a sign does not need to go first, and the verse makes that confidence visible. His calm is a contrast to the bargaining that has just taken place, and it prepares the reader for the moment when the two performances meet.

phrases.translation: So they cast down their ropes and staffs,
phrases.explanation: The magicians perform. They cast down their ropes and staffs, and the commentary explains that they threw them from their hands in the sight of the assembled crowd. What the spectators saw looked like movement and life, which was the whole art. The verse describes the act without yet judging it, so that the reader experiences the same moment of uncertainty as the crowd before the next verse resolves it.

phrases.translation: saying, “By Pharaoh’s might, it is we who will surely prevail.”
phrases.explanation: Their words are then reported. By Pharaoh's might, it is we who will surely prevail, and the commentary explains that they swore by the power and severity of Pharaoh's authority and the security of his kingship. The oath names the real object of their confidence. They do not invoke any god but the king whose court pays them, which shows that the contest has never been between two kinds of magic but between two kinds of reliance.

phrases.translation: Then Moses threw down his staff,
phrases.explanation: Moses acts after they have finished. Then Moses threw down his staff, and the commentary notes that he did so only after the sorcerers had thrown theirs. The order matters because it lets the illusion occupy the field first. There is no hurry and no attempt to match their display, and the single gesture is the same one he had used in the palace hall.

phrases.translation: and—behold!—it devoured the objects of their illusion
phrases.explanation: The result is described in a word. Behold, it devoured the objects of their illusion, and the commentary explains this as the staff swallowing the falsehood and sorcery they had produced, which had no reality behind it and was only appearances and deception. What looked impressive is eaten by what is real. The verse names their work as illusion without denying that it was seen, and it settles the contest in a way no amount of skill could answer.

phrases.translation: So the magicians fell down, prostrating
phrases.explanation: The verse records what the magicians did when the staff swallowed their work. They fell down prostrating, and the commentary explains that when it became clear to them that what Moses had brought was the truth and not sorcery, and that it was something no one could do except Allah, they dropped on their faces in obedience. The men who had sworn by Pharaoh's might were on the ground before another authority. The verse puts the body first, since their conversion happened on seeing.

phrases.translation: They declared, “We ˹now˺ believe in the Lord of all worlds—
phrases.explanation: Their confession is then reported. They declared, we now believe in the Lord of all worlds, and the commentary explains this as the God to whom Moses had called them, in place of Pharaoh and his nobles. The formula takes up the very words Pharaoh had mocked earlier when he asked what the Lord of all worlds was. The court's joke has become the prisoners' creed, spoken in the same hall and before the same king.

phrases.translation: the Lord of Moses and Aaron.”
phrases.explanation: The verse completes the confession with two names. The Lord of Moses and Aaron, they say, and the commentary explains that this identifies the Lord of all worlds with the God of the two brothers, so that no doubt remains about whom they mean. Naming the messengers ties the confession to the men standing in front of them. A general phrase about the Lord of everything is now anchored in a particular mission, which is what makes it dangerous to say in Egypt.

phrases.translation: Pharaoh threatened, “How dare you believe in him before I give you permission?
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh answers with outrage at the timing. How dare you believe in him before I give you permission, and the commentary explains the offence as belief in Moses without the king's leave. The complaint is about authority rather than about truth, since he does not deny that the sign happened. A ruler who has just been defeated by a staff now insists on controlling who may draw conclusions from it.

phrases.translation: He must be your master who taught you magic, but soon
phrases.explanation: He then explains their conversion as a conspiracy. He must be your master who taught you magic, and the commentary explains this as Pharaoh claiming that Moses was their leader in sorcery and had taught them the craft, which is why they believed in him. The accusation preserves his own position by turning the defeat into collusion. Anyone watching would see that the king has no account of the sign itself.

phrases.translation: you will see. I will certainly cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides, then crucify you all.”
phrases.explanation: The threat is then spelled out. I will cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides, then crucify you all, and the commentary explains the punishment as cutting the right hand and the left foot and so on from opposite sides, and crucifying every one of them without exception. The sentence is designed to be public and slow. Power that cannot answer an argument falls back on making an example, and the verse shows the exact moment a regime stops pretending to reason.

phrases.translation: They responded, “˹That would be˺ no harm!
phrases.explanation: The magicians answer without flinching. That would be no harm, they say, and the commentary explains the phrase as meaning that whatever he did to them and however he crucified them, it would not injure them. The reply reverses the meaning of punishment. What the king intends as the worst thing that can happen has become something they can absorb, and their calm is a greater defeat for him than the loss of the contest.

phrases.translation: Surely to our Lord we will ˹all˺ return
phrases.explanation: The reason for that calm is then given. Surely to our Lord we will all return, and the commentary explains this as their certainty of returning to Allah, who would reward them for their patience under his punishment and for their steadfastness in His oneness. The whole threat depended on death being the end, and they had just learned that it is not. A man who expects to stand before his Lord cannot be frightened by a king who will also have to stand there.

phrases.translation: We really hope that our Lord will forgive our sins,
phrases.explanation: The verse gives their hope a specific content. We really hope that our Lord will forgive our sins, and the commentary explains the hope as their expectation that Allah would forgive what they had done before believing, including the sorcery and the disbelief in which they had lived. They do not claim innocence but ask for pardon. The men who had been hired to defend a false god now ask mercy for the craft they had practiced in his service.

phrases.translation: as we are the first to believe.”
phrases.explanation: The ground of that hope is then named. As we are the first to believe, and the commentary explains this as their being the first to believe in Moses and confirm what he brought in that time. The phrase is not a boast about rank but an appeal to what they had just sacrificed. They had given up their position and their safety at the first sight of the truth, and they ask that this be counted.

phrases.translation: And We inspired Moses, ˹saying,˺ “Leave with My servants at night,
phrases.explanation: The scene changes with a command from Allah. We inspired Moses, saying, leave with My servants at night, and the commentary explains this as the instruction given after Pharaoh had persisted in his folly and refused to stop despite the signs shown to him. The word servants names the Children of Israel as belonging to Allah rather than to the king who held them. A departure is ordered that no negotiation could have achieved.

phrases.translation: for you will surely be pursued.”
phrases.explanation: The command ends with a warning that removes any hope of a quiet exit. For you will surely be pursued, and the commentary explains this as the pursuit by Pharaoh and his armies, who would come after them to stop them from leaving Egypt. The escape will not be a secret. The verse tells Moses in advance that the road out will be crowded behind him, so that what happens at the sea is understood as a planned deliverance rather than a fortunate accident.

phrases.translation: Then Pharaoh sent mobilizers to all cities
phrases.explanation: The verse shows the response to the escape. Pharaoh sent mobilizers to all cities, and the commentary explains that he sent messengers through the towns to gather his army and his people for him. The same machinery that had been used to collect magicians is now used to collect soldiers. A kingdom is being assembled to chase a group of former slaves, and the scale of the reaction measures how much the departure threatened the order of Egypt.

phrases.translation: ˹and said,˺ “These ˹outcasts˺ are just a handful of people
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh describes the fugitives to his own people. These outcasts are just a handful of people, and the commentary explains the term as a small remnant left over from larger groups, and records a report that this handful numbered six hundred and seventy thousand men. The description is meant to belittle and to reassure. A king addressing an army has to make the enemy seem small, and the verse preserves the words he used to do it.

phrases.translation: who have really enraged us
phrases.explanation: The verse gives the second half of the complaint. Who have really enraged us, and the commentary explains this as the claim that this small band had provoked the anger of Pharaoh's people. It records explanations of that anger, including the killing of their firstborn among people and cattle, the departure with goods borrowed from the Egyptians, and the humiliation of seeing them leave despite the court's refusal. The grievance is real, which is why the pursuit could be presented as justified.

phrases.translation: but we are all on the alert.”
phrases.explanation: The speech ends with a claim of readiness. But we are all on the alert, and the commentary explains the word as meaning that they were prepared, equipped, and in possession of weapons and strength, and notes that reciters differ over whether it describes a state of vigilance or a settled habit of caution. Either way the contrast is deliberate. A handful of frightened people against a kingdom fully armed is the picture Pharaoh wants his troops to hold.

phrases.translation: So We lured the tyrants out of ˹their˺ gardens, springs
phrases.explanation: The verse turns the picture around. So We lured the tyrants out of their gardens and springs, and the commentary explains this as Allah bringing Pharaoh and his people out of the gardens and the flowing waters they possessed. The word is taken from hunting, where game is drawn from cover. What looked like a pursuit mounted by a confident king is described as a removal arranged by another hand, and the wealth they left behind becomes the subject of the next verses.

phrases.translation: treasures, and splendid residences
phrases.explanation: The list of what they left continues. Treasures and splendid residences, and the commentary explains the treasures as gold and silver and the residences as an honourable dwelling, with a report that these were the raised seats or pulpits of the court. The verse piles up what Egypt could offer, because the point is the size of the loss. A people who would not release a nation for Allah's sake lose the gardens and the houses they were unwilling to leave.

phrases.translation: So it was. And We awarded it ˹all˺ to the Children of Israel
phrases.explanation: The verse marks the completion of the transfer and names the new owners. So it was, it begins, confirming that everything described happened as stated, and then it says that Allah awarded it all to the Children of Israel, meaning the gardens, springs, treasures, and dwellings of those from whom they had been taken out. The slaves receive the estate of their masters. The verse answers Pharaoh's claim that Moses wanted to drive out the nobles, since the departure became inheritance rather than theft.

phrases.translation: And so they pursued them at sunrise
phrases.explanation: The verse reports the pursuit and fixes its time. And so they pursued them at sunrise, and the commentary explains this as Pharaoh and his companions following the Children of Israel at the break of morning. The detail is exact because the Exodus was remembered by its hours. A night departure had been commanded, and the chase begins when the light returns, so that the two hosts will meet in the open where nothing can be hidden.

phrases.translation: When the two groups came face to face,
phrases.explanation: The two sides finally see each other. When the two groups came face to face, and the commentary explains the two hosts as the people of Moses, meaning the Children of Israel, and the people of Pharaoh, meaning the Copts. The moment is described from the side of the weaker party, who have the sea ahead and the army behind. Everything the narrative has been building toward rests on the next few words.

phrases.translation: the companions of Moses cried out, “We are overtaken for sure.”
phrases.explanation: Their cry is quoted. We are overtaken for sure, and the commentary explains this as their certainty that Pharaoh and his armies would now reach them and kill them. It also records that they said this to Moses himself, treating him as an evil omen and complaining that they had been oppressed before he came and after he came. The people who had walked out by night now calculate the odds, and the odds are entirely against them.

phrases.translation: Moses reassured ˹them˺, “Absolutely not! My Lord is certainly with me—He will guide me.”
phrases.explanation: Moses answers with a denial resting on presence rather than numbers. Absolutely not, he says, my Lord is certainly with me, He will guide me, and the commentary explains this as his assurance that they would not be overtaken and that Allah would show him the way of escape. One report adds that Allah had promised him deliverance and that there is no contradiction in His promise. The leader is certain where the crowd is not, and he does not yet know the plan either.

phrases.translation: So We inspired Moses: “Strike the sea with your staff,”
phrases.explanation: The command comes at the last moment. Strike the sea with your staff, Moses is told, and the commentary explains that the sea had been commanded not to split until it was struck with that staff. One report describes Aaron striking and the sea refusing, until Moses addressed it and struck. The instrument is the same one that became a serpent in the palace. The way out is the sea obeying a command, not a path anyone could have arranged.

phrases.translation: and the sea was split, each part was like a huge mountain
phrases.explanation: The result is then described. The sea was split, each part like a huge mountain, and the commentary explains the image as the water standing in walls on either side. What had been a barrier becomes a road with heights on both sides. The verse gives the reader the scale of the thing before the next verses show the pursuers entering it, so that the path and the trap are understood to be the same water.

phrases.translation: We drew the pursuers to that place
phrases.explanation: The verse reports what happened to the other side. We drew the pursuers to that place, and the commentary explains this as Allah bringing the people of Pharaoh near and driving them toward the sea. The same providence that opened the way is described as closing the distance behind it. Nothing is said yet about what will happen to them, and the restraint makes the next two verses read as an answer rather than an ambush.

phrases.translation: and delivered Moses and those with him all together
phrases.explanation: The verse states the first half of the outcome. And delivered Moses and those with him all together, and the commentary explains this as saving Moses from the drowning that overtook Pharaoh and his people, along with everyone who had left Egypt with him. The phrase all together matters, since not one of the fugitives was lost. A crowd that had just said it was overtaken is now entirely safe, and the deliverance covers the weakest among them as well as the leader.

phrases.translation: Then We drowned the others
phrases.explanation: The verse states the second half. Then We drowned the others, and the commentary explains this as the drowning of Pharaoh and his Coptic people in the sea after Moses and his companions had been saved from it. The two sentences are placed in order, deliverance first and destruction second, so that the reader sees them as one act. The army that had been gathered from every city to chase a handful of people disappears in the water it had entered.

phrases.translation: Surely in this is a sign. Yet most of them would not believe
phrases.explanation: The refrain returns after the destruction. Surely in this is a sign, and the commentary explains the sign as the drowning of Pharaoh and his companions for denying Moses, a proof for the people of Quraysh that this is how Allah deals with those who deny His messengers, and an admonition so that they do not do the same. It also draws out the other half, that the rescue of Moses is a sign of what patience brings. The verse holds warning and promise together.

phrases.translation: And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The verse names the two qualities that explain the account. Your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful, and the commentary explains the first as His vengeance against those who deny His messengers, and the second as His mercy toward the messengers and their followers whom He saved. The same event shows both, since the water that destroyed one side carried the other through. The verse keeps severity and mercy from being separated.

phrases.translation: Relate to them ˹O Prophet˺ the story of Abraham
phrases.explanation: A new narrative is introduced. Relate to them the story of Abraham, and the commentary explains the command as addressed to the Prophet, that he should recount to his people of the polytheists the story of Ibrahim. The choice is pointed, since the Quraysh traced their lineage and their sanctuary to him. The chapter now turns from a nation destroyed to an ancestor the hearers claimed, and asks them to hear what he actually did with idols.

phrases.translation: when he questioned his father and his people,
phrases.explanation: The story begins with a question. When he questioned his father and his people, and the commentary explains that he put this to them directly rather than arguing behind their backs. The scene is a family and a community confronted by one of their own. Abraham is not shown debating philosophers but asking the people who raised him what they were doing, which makes the question sharper than any lecture.

phrases.translation: “What is that you worship ˹besides Allah˺?”
phrases.explanation: The question is then quoted. What is that you worship besides Allah, and the commentary explains it as his asking what these objects were that they served. The word for that is a request for identification rather than for doctrine. He does not begin by denying their gods but by making them say aloud what those gods are, which is the first step toward seeing that they are nothing.

phrases.translation: They replied, “We worship idols,
phrases.explanation: Their answer is frank and unembarrassed. We worship idols, they reply, and the commentary explains the word as images they served. It is not a defence and not an explanation, only a statement of practice. The reply shows that the question had never occurred to them before, since they answer with what they do rather than with any reason for doing it.

phrases.translation: to which we are fully devoted.”
phrases.explanation: The second half shows the devotion they take pride in. To which we are fully devoted, they say, and the commentary explains the phrase as their abiding beside the idols in continual service and prayer. It records one report that this meant the prayer they offered to them. The word describes a settled attendance, a habit rather than a conviction. Their religion is presented as loyalty to objects that cannot respond.

phrases.translation: Abraham asked, “Can they hear you when you call upon them
phrases.explanation: Abraham tests the devotion with a simple question. Can they hear you when you call upon them, and the commentary explains this as asking whether the gods hear those who invoke them, with the sense of hearing their calling. The question is deliberately modest, since hearing is the least a god would need to do. He does not ask whether they can create or provide, only whether they notice that someone is speaking, and the answer is already implied in the silence that follows.

phrases.translation: Or can they benefit or harm you?”
phrases.explanation: The question widens to benefit and harm. Or can they benefit or harm you, and the commentary explains this as asking whether the idols give anything in return for worship or punish its neglect. The two questions cover the whole case for worship, that a god hears and that a god acts. Since the idols do neither, the devotion described before is loyalty without an object, and the next verse gives the only answer the people had.

phrases.translation: They replied, “No! But we found our forefathers doing the same.”
phrases.explanation: The answer concedes everything and changes nothing. No, they reply, but we found our forefathers doing the same, and the commentary explains the first word as a turning back from what had been denied, that the idols do not hear and do not benefit, followed by the only reason they had. The verse records a religion defended by inheritance alone. They do not claim that the idols are anything. They claim only that their fathers thought so, which is the whole of their case.

phrases.translation: Abraham responded, “Have you ˹really˺ considered what you have been worshipping—
phrases.explanation: Abraham answers that inheritance. Have you really considered what you have been worshipping, he asks, and the commentary explains the question as an invitation to look carefully at the objects themselves and at what their worship amounts to. The word considered implies a judgement still to be made. Having been told that the practice came from the ancestors, he asks them to examine it now for themselves, which is exactly what they had never done.

phrases.translation: you and your ancestors
phrases.explanation: The question is extended to the generations behind them. You and your ancestors, and the commentary explains this as including the earliest forefathers who had been in the same condition of idol worship. The verse does not exempt age from scrutiny. A practice does not become true by being old, and Abraham names the whole chain so that no part of it can be sheltered behind the other.

phrases.translation: They are ˹all˺ enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The conclusion is stated with a surprising word. They are all enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds, and the commentary explains the difficulty, since wood and stone cannot be anyone's enemy, and answers that they would be his enemies on the Day of Resurrection, as another verse says that the gods taken besides Allah will deny their worshippers and become their adversaries. The break is complete. Everything worshipped besides Allah is on the other side, including the idols of his own father.

phrases.translation: ˹He is˺ the One Who created me, and He ˹alone˺ guides me
phrases.explanation: The exception is then described by what Allah does. He is the One Who created me, and He alone guides me, and the commentary explains the guidance as being shown what is right in word and deed and led to the straight path. Creation and direction are placed together because the One who began a life is the one who knows where it should go. The verse begins a list of personal dealings that runs to the end of the passage.

phrases.translation: ˹He is˺ the One Who provides me with food and drink
phrases.explanation: The list continues with daily provision. He is the One Who provides me with food and drink, and the commentary explains this as Allah feeding him and giving him drink and bestowing provision upon him. The claim is not about rare gifts but about the ordinary means of staying alive. Abraham names the things that arrive every day without being arranged by the one who receives them, and by naming them he turns a routine into evidence.

phrases.translation: And He ˹alone˺ heals me when I am sick
phrases.explanation: The verse adds the healing that follows illness. And He alone heals me when I am sick, and the commentary explains this as Allah restoring the body when it grows weak. The wording is careful, since the illness is attributed to the servant and the healing to Allah alone. Abraham does not say that his Lord makes him sick but that when sickness comes his Lord is the one who removes it, which is both a confession of dependence and a refusal to blame.

phrases.translation: And He ˹is the One Who˺ will cause me to die, and then bring me back to life
phrases.explanation: The list reaches its end. And He is the One Who will cause me to die, and then bring me back to life, and the commentary explains this as Allah causing his death when He wills and raising him after death when He wishes. It names the one act no idol could perform for a worshipper. Everything before this was about food, healing, and guidance within a life, and this is about the end of that life, where the argument against the idols becomes absolute.

phrases.translation: And He is ˹the One˺ Who, I hope, will forgive my flaws on Judgment Day.”
phrases.explanation: The last item is a hope rather than a claim. And He is the One Who, I hope, will forgive my flaws on Judgment Day, and the commentary explains that the list is an argument against his people, since worship belongs only to the One who does these things, not to what cannot benefit or harm. It records that the flaw he meant was a slip of speech. Even a prophet needs pardon, and the verse closes the case against gods who give nothing.

phrases.translation: “My Lord! Grant me wisdom, and join me with the righteous
phrases.explanation: A new prayer begins. My Lord, grant me wisdom, and join me with the righteous, and the commentary explains the wisdom as prophethood and the joining as being made a messenger to Allah's creation and placed among those He sent with His revelation. The request is not for comfort but for a place in a line of messengers. Having declared himself free of the idols of his people, Abraham asks for company of a different kind and for the work that goes with it.

phrases.translation: Bless me with honourable mention among later generations
phrases.explanation: The prayer turns to what will be said of him later. Bless me with honourable mention among later generations, and the commentary explains this as asking for a fair remembrance and good praise lasting among the generations to come. It records a report that he asked this so the nations would not deny him. The request is unusual because it concerns a reputation that outlives him, and it is granted in the communities who later claimed him as their father in faith.

phrases.translation: Make me one of those awarded the Garden of Bliss
phrases.explanation: The next request concerns the world to come. Make me one of those awarded the Garden of Bliss, and the commentary explains this as asking to inherit dwellings in Paradise among those of the polytheists who perished, and to dwell in them. The image is of an inheritance rather than a purchase. The man who left his people and their gods asks for a place among the heirs of what those gods could never give.

phrases.translation: Forgive my father, for he is certainly one of the misguided
phrases.explanation: The prayer asks pardon for his father. Forgive my father, for he is certainly one of the misguided, and the commentary explains this as asking Allah to overlook his father's worship of other gods and not to punish him, while naming him as one who strayed into disbelief. The verse joins a request for mercy with a plain statement of the man's error. Abraham does not pretend his father was right, and he does not stop caring for him.

phrases.translation: And do not disgrace me on the Day all will be resurrected—
phrases.explanation: The prayer ends with a plea about the last day. And do not disgrace me on the Day all will be resurrected, and the commentary explains this as asking not to be shamed by punishment on the day when Allah raises His servants from their graves. The word disgrace is about exposure rather than pain. Having asked for wisdom, a good name, Paradise, and his father's pardon, he closes by asking that none of it be taken away in public.

phrases.translation: the Day when neither wealth nor children will be of any benefit
phrases.explanation: The verse names what the day will not value. The Day when neither wealth nor children will be of any benefit, and the commentary explains this as the day when a disbeliever gains nothing from his wealth or his sons, since neither will ward off punishment or rescue him. The two things people trust most are exactly what will not be counted. In a society that measured a man by property and sons, the verse removes both at once.

phrases.translation: Only those who come before Allah with a pure heart ˹will be saved˺.”
phrases.explanation: The exception is then stated. Only those who come before Allah with a pure heart, and the commentary explains the purity as freedom from doubt about the oneness of Allah and the resurrection after death. It records that the sound heart knows Allah is the truth, that the Hour is coming, and that He will raise those in the graves. What survives the day is not an achievement but a condition of the heart, and the passage about Abraham has been building toward it.

phrases.translation: ˹On that Day˺ Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing
phrases.explanation: The scene widens to the two destinations. On that Day Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing, and the commentary explains this as the garden being drawn close to those who feared Allah's punishment in the next life and obeyed Him in this one. The nearness is the reward, since the garden is not merely entered but brought to them. Having described what will not help, the verse shows what will, and it is a quality of life rather than a quantity of possessions.

phrases.translation: and the Hellfire will be displayed to the deviant
phrases.explanation: The other destination is then shown. And the Hellfire will be displayed to the deviant, and the commentary explains this as the fire being made manifest to those who went astray and left the straight path. The two verses are matched, one bringing the garden near and the other uncovering the fire. Nothing is hidden on that day, and what each group had been moving toward all along is finally placed in front of them.

phrases.translation: And it will be said to them, “Where are those you used to worship
phrases.explanation: A question is put to them. It will be said, where are those you used to worship, and the commentary explains that this was addressed to the erring ones and that the question concerns the equals they had set up. The mocking question Pharaoh asked about the Lord of all worlds is now asked of them about their own gods. The verse makes their worship look like what it was, an absence, and the fire before them is the only answer.

phrases.translation: besides Allah? Can they help you or even help themselves?”
phrases.explanation: The question is completed with a challenge. Besides Allah, can they help you or even help themselves, and the commentary explains the two halves as asking whether the gods can rescue their worshippers from punishment and whether they can save themselves from what awaits them. The second is the harder blow, since a god that cannot protect itself can hardly protect anyone. The idols who could not hear in this world are now shown to be helpless in the next.

phrases.translation: Then the idols will be hurled headlong into Hell, along with the deviant
phrases.explanation: The end of that exchange is then described. Then the idols will be hurled headlong into Hell, along with the deviant, and the commentary explains the word as being flung down one upon another, thrown face first into the fire in a heap. It notes that the word is a doubled form of the ordinary verb for casting down. Worshippers and worshipped fall together, which is the collapse of a religion whose gods cannot stay out of the fire their devotees enter.

phrases.translation: and the soldiers of Iblîs, all together
phrases.explanation: The list of the fallen is completed. And the soldiers of Iblis, all together, and the commentary explains this as his hosts being cast into the fire along with the gods and the misguided, defining those hosts as everyone who followed him, whether from his own offspring or from the children of Adam. The verse reaches the source of the misguidance. Behind the idols and the worshippers stands the one who urged the worship, and he does not escape what he sold them.

phrases.translation: There the deviant will cry while disputing with their idols
phrases.explanation: The verse shows what happens among them in the fire. There the deviant will cry while disputing with their idols, and the commentary explains that the misguided, the gods they served, and the hosts of Iblis all speak this way as they argue with one another in the blazing fire. The blaming is mutual, the last form of a partnership built on falsehood. The worshippers cannot plead ignorance of the gods, since the gods are there and have nothing to offer in their defence.

phrases.translation: “By Allah! We were clearly mistaken
phrases.explanation: The confession is quoted with an oath. By Allah, they say, we were clearly mistaken, and the commentary explains this as their admitting that they had strayed from the truth and that their error was manifest to anyone who beheld it, being visibly remote from the truth. What they refused to hear from a messenger they now see for themselves. The verse gives them clarity at the moment when clarity can no longer help.

phrases.translation: when we made you equal to the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The verse names the error precisely. When we made you equal to the Lord of all worlds, and the commentary explains this as the misguided saying to the gods they had served that they were in plain error when they set them equal to Allah and worshipped them beside Him. The sin is not denial of a Lord but the joining of others to Him. Their confession identifies the exact fault, which means that on that day nobody is confused about what went wrong.

phrases.translation: And none led us astray other than the wicked
phrases.explanation: The confession turns to blame. And none led us astray other than the wicked, and the commentary explains the criminals meant here as Iblis and the son of Adam who first established killing, with a report naming both. The verse gathers the leaders of every evil into a single category. Having admitted their own error, they now name who drew them into it, which is a true statement but not a defence, since they had followed with their eyes open.

phrases.translation: Now we have none to intercede for us
phrases.explanation: They then state what they lack. Now we have none to intercede for us, and the commentary explains this as their having no intercessor who could plead with Allah on their behalf and save them from punishment. Everything people rely on at court is gone, since there is no patron to speak for them. The verse follows the naming of those who misled them with the discovery that no ally remains, and the two together leave them entirely alone.

phrases.translation: nor a close friend
phrases.explanation: The verse adds the second absence. Nor a close friend, and the commentary explains the phrase as a devoted friend from among close relatives, and records views that the intercessors are the angels and the friend a blood relative, or that both are from the descendants of Adam. The word describes affection that is sincere and warm. In a place where no advocacy and no friendship can reach, the world that sustained them is shown to have been worth nothing.

phrases.translation: If only we could have a second chance, then we would be believers.”
phrases.explanation: Their last words are a wish that cannot be granted. If only we could have a second chance, then we would be believers, and the commentary explains this as their longing for a return to the world so that they might believe in Allah. The verse does not say the wish was refused, because it does not need to. Everything they ask for is what they were offered and refused, and the wish proves that they now know it.

phrases.translation: Surely in this is a sign. Yet most of them would not believe
phrases.explanation: The refrain returns after Abraham's story. Surely in this is a sign, and the commentary explains the sign as the proofs Abraham set out, from which it is clear that Allah's way with those who worship idols is the same as what He will do in the next life, when they and their gods are cast into the fire. Yet most of them would not believe. The verse closes the narrative by joining the ancient argument to the present hearers.

phrases.translation: And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The verse names the two qualities again. Your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful, and the commentary explains the first as severe retribution for whoever worships something besides Him and dies without repenting, and the second as mercy toward whoever does repent, so that his past is not punished. The pair keeps the warning from becoming despair. Even after the scene of the fire and the failed wish, the door is described as open for the one who turns back now.

phrases.translation: The people of Noah rejected the messengers
phrases.explanation: A third narrative begins. The people of Noah rejected the messengers, and the commentary explains this as their denial of the messengers Allah had sent to them. The plural is used although one man was sent, because every messenger brings the same message and to reject one is to reject the line. The verse states the verdict before the story, which makes the account that follows an illustration of a conclusion already drawn.

phrases.translation: when their brother Noah said to them, “Will you not fear ˹Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The story opens with the appeal. When their brother Noah said to them, will you not fear Allah, and the commentary explains the question as asking whether they would not fear His punishment for their disbelief and their rejection of His messengers. The word brother matters, since he was one of them and not a stranger. The first thing he says is not a doctrine but a question about fear, which leaves room for them to answer.

phrases.translation: I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you
phrases.explanation: He then states his standing among them. I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you, and the commentary explains the trustworthiness as his being faithful with the revelation given to him and the message he was sent to deliver. The claim is about honesty rather than authority, which is what a people who had known him all his life could actually test. Before asking them to accept anything, he asks them to consider whether he had ever lied to them.

phrases.translation: So fear Allah, and obey me
phrases.explanation: The two commands follow. So fear Allah, and obey me, and the commentary explains the first as fearing His punishment for disbelief and the second as obeying Noah in his counsel and in his command to fear Him. Obedience is asked for in the specific matter of the warning, not in everything. The words are brief because the message is: turn from what you are doing and accept the one who brought it, and everything else in the chapter will test whether that was refused.

phrases.translation: I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺.
phrases.explanation: Noah states the terms of his service. I do not ask you for any reward for this message, and the commentary explains this as his seeking no payment or wage for the counsel he gave them and his command that they fear Allah's punishment. The verse removes the suspicion that a prophet is working for gain, which is the first thing a wealthy town would assume about a man who asks it to change.

phrases.translation: My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The second half names where payment comes from. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds, and the commentary explains this as his wage resting with Allah and not with them or with any creature. The word only shuts the door on every other patron. A messenger paid by his people can be bought or dismissed, and Noah declares at the outset that he is neither, which leaves them with nothing to bargain with.

phrases.translation: So fear Allah, and obey me.”
phrases.explanation: The verse repeats the call. So fear Allah, and obey me, and the commentary explains this as fearing His punishment for disbelief and the descent of His wrath for rejecting His messengers, and obeying Noah in his counsel and his call to worship the Creator alone. The repetition is deliberate, since the same two commands frame the offer of no reward. What he wants is not money but obedience to the One who sent him, and his first speech ends where it began.

phrases.translation: They argued, “How can we believe in you,
phrases.explanation: The people answer with the objection of the powerful. How can we believe in you, they ask, and the commentary explains the question as their refusal to accept Noah's truthfulness in what he called them to. The objection is not about evidence but about company. They are asking how a message could be true if it has not persuaded the people whose opinion they valued, which is a way of letting social standing decide a question of fact.

phrases.translation: when you are followed ˹only˺ by the lowest of the low?”
phrases.explanation: The second half states the complaint plainly. When you are followed only by the lowest of the low, and the commentary explains this as their pointing out that only the lowly had followed him and not the people of standing and the prominent families. The verse shows exactly what stood between them and belief. It was not the argument but the guest list, and the men who considered themselves the weight of the town would not join a movement whose members they looked down on.

phrases.translation: He responded, “And what knowledge do I have of what they do
phrases.explanation: Noah refuses to judge what he cannot see. What knowledge do I have of what they do, he asks, and the commentary explains this as his knowing only the outward appearance of his followers, since he was not charged with knowledge of their inner state, thinking well of whoever outwardly does good and ill of whoever does evil.
