The accounting of their hearts belongs to his Lord. The answer moves the question from status to what only Allah can read.

phrases.translation: Their judgment is with my Lord, if you had any sense
phrases.explanation: The verse states the conclusion of that answer. Their judgment is with my Lord, if you had any sense, and the commentary explains this as the accounting for what is hidden in their souls resting with Allah alone. The conditional rebuke is addressed to people who have just measured their neighbours by wealth and family. Noah tells them that the judgement they are making so confidently belongs to someone else, and that the sense they pride themselves on is not being used.

phrases.translation: I am not going to expel the believers
phrases.explanation: The refusal is made explicit. I am not going to expel the believers, and the commentary explains this as Noah telling his people that he will not drive away those who believed in Allah and followed him. The demand behind their objection was that he clear out the poor to make room for the respectable. The verse shows a messenger refusing to trade his weakest followers for the goodwill of the strongest, and the whole scene turns on that point.

phrases.translation: I am only sent with a clear warning.”
phrases.explanation: The verse gives his actual office. I am only sent with a clear warning, and the commentary explains this as his being a warner from his Lord, warning them of His severity and His grip, and clear in the sense that his warning had become plain and he had hidden nothing of his counsel. The word only limits what he can do. He cannot expel people or compel belief, because he was sent to speak and not to sort.

phrases.translation: They threatened, “If you do not desist, O Noah,
phrases.explanation: The reply is a threat. They said that if he did not desist, O Noah, and the commentary explains this as their demand that he stop saying what he said and stop calling them to it, since he was reviling their gods. The condition is telling, because they do not ask him to prove anything or answer his argument. They ask only that he be quiet, which is what a case looks like when it has no answer left.

phrases.translation: you will surely be stoned ˹to death˺.”
phrases.explanation: The threat is then named. You will surely be stoned to death, and the commentary explains the word as their promise to revile him, that he would be among those whom they cursed and abused. Whether the word means stones or insults, the intent is the same, to make speech too costly to continue. The verse shows the moment the argument ends and social violence begins, and it is the point at which the prophet stops addressing them and turns to his Lord.

phrases.translation: Noah prayed, “My Lord! My people have truly rejected me
phrases.explanation: Noah turns from the people to his Lord. My Lord, my people have truly rejected me, he says, and the commentary explains this as his complaint that they had denied the truth he brought and rejected his counsel. The words are plain and without elaboration. Having spent the scene refusing to bargain and refusing to expel his followers, he now states the situation to the One who can do something about it, and the prayer is short because the case is already clear.

phrases.translation: So judge between me and them decisively,
phrases.explanation: The request is for a judgement, not a favour. So judge between me and them decisively, and the commentary explains this as asking Allah to judge in a way that destroys the party of falsehood and takes vengeance on those who disbelieve and reject His messenger. Noah does not ask for a lighter sentence on them but for the matter to be settled. The word carries the sense of a decision that opens the way, the language of a man who has finished arguing.

phrases.translation: and save me and the believers with me.”
phrases.explanation: The second half includes those with him. And save me and the believers with me, and the commentary explains this as asking to be delivered from the punishment sent as a judgement, along with those who believed in Allah and affirmed him. The prayer joins his own rescue to the rescue of the small group he had refused to abandon. Everything he would not trade away in the previous scene is now named in his final request, and the answer is the ark.

phrases.translation: So We saved him and those with him in the fully loaded Ark
phrases.explanation: The answer is described in one sentence. So We saved him and those with him in the fully loaded Ark, and the commentary explains the ship as one loaded and filled almost to sinking, with reports glossing the word as heavily laden. The detail is practical, since a crowded boat is a small community carried through water that destroys everyone outside. The believers Noah would not expel are the ones saved, and the ark holds exactly those who accepted the warning.

phrases.translation: Then afterwards We drowned the rest
phrases.explanation: The verse states the other half of the judgement. Then afterwards We drowned the rest, and the commentary explains this as the remaining members of his people who had denied him and rejected his counsel. The order is the same as in the account of Pharaoh, rescue first and destruction after. The people who would not stop the preaching are stopped by the water, and the verse says it in six words, since the argument has already been made and only the outcome remains.

phrases.translation: Surely in this is a sign. Yet most of them would not believe
phrases.explanation: The refrain closes the Noah narrative. Surely in this is a sign, and the commentary explains the sign as what was done to Noah and those with him, a proof for the Prophet and his people that it is Allah's custom to save His messengers and their followers when punishment descends on those who deny them, and that this custom applies to the present hearers too. Yet most of them would not believe. The verse makes the ancient story a warning aimed at Mecca.

phrases.translation: And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The verse again names the two qualities. Your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful, and the commentary explains the first as His vengeance on those who disbelieve and transgress His command, and the second as His mercy toward the repentant, so that he is not punished after turning back. The pair appears after every destroyed people, keeping the chapter from becoming a list of disasters. The Lord who drowned the deniers is ready to pardon anyone who stops denying.

phrases.translation: The people of ’Âd rejected the messengers
phrases.explanation: A fourth people is introduced in the same words. The people of Ad rejected the messengers, and the commentary explains this as their denial of the messengers Allah had sent to them. Ad were a nation remembered for strength and for the ruins of their towers, and the chapter has already listed them among the destroyed. The verse begins the account the same way as the others so that the pattern is felt before the details arrive.

phrases.translation: when their brother Hûd said to them, “Will you not fear ˹Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The appeal is identical to Noah's. When their brother Hud said to them, will you not fear Allah, and the commentary explains the question as asking whether they would not fear His punishment for their disbelief. The repetition is the point, since a different people, a different age, and a different prophet arrive at the same first word. The messenger is called their brother, one of their own, and he opens not with a demand for obedience but with a question about fear.

phrases.translation: I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you
phrases.explanation: Hud states his standing among them. I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you, and the commentary explains this as his being sent from his Lord who commands obedience and warns of His severity, and trustworthy with respect to the revelation and the message entrusted to him. The claim is about reliability in delivery rather than about authority. For a people who had known him all their lives, the only thing to test was whether he had ever lied.

phrases.translation: So fear Allah, and obey me
phrases.explanation: The two commands follow the claim. So fear Allah, and obey me, and the commentary explains the first as obeying Allah in what He commands and forbids, and the second as obeying Hud in what he commands, namely the fear of Allah and the acceptance of his warning. The words are short because the message is short. Everything in the passage depends on whether a people proud of their strength will accept a warning from one of their own.

phrases.translation: I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺.
phrases.explanation: He then removes any question of payment. I do not ask you for any reward for this message, and the commentary explains this as his seeking no recompense for charging them to fear Allah. The verse answers an accusation before it is made, since a wealthy and powerful people would suspect a reformer of wanting their wealth. A man who wants nothing from them cannot be bought, dismissed, or accused of trading on his message.

phrases.translation: My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The second half says where his wage rests. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds, and the commentary explains this as his recompense for sincere counsel resting solely with Allah. The word only closes the account with every other payer. Noah had said the same thing in the previous narrative, and the repetition shows that this is not a personal style but the standing condition of a messenger, who must be free of the people he is sent to correct.

phrases.translation: ˹Why˺ do you build a landmark
phrases.explanation: Hud turns to what they were doing with their strength. Why do you build a landmark, he asks, and the commentary explains the word as every high and elevated place on the earth, and the verse as a question about raising a monument on each height. The question is not about architecture but about purpose. A people with power will spend it on display, and Hud begins with the habit rather than with the sin.

phrases.translation: on every high place in vanity
phrases.explanation: The purpose is then named. On every high place in vanity, and the commentary explains the phrase as building for amusement rather than for use. The accusation is that the work was play, undertaken to be seen and to pass the time. The verse lets the reader picture a nation erecting markers across a landscape, and asks what all that building was for when nobody needed the buildings.

phrases.translation: and construct castles, as if you are going to live forever
phrases.explanation: The second charge is more serious. And construct castles, as if you are going to live forever, and the commentary explains the castles as lofty palaces and durable buildings, and records a report describing them as fortresses and palaces built on the hope of living on. The verse names the illusion behind the architecture. Ad were strong enough to build for permanence, and the chapter has already told the reader that they were destroyed, which is the answer to the hope the buildings expressed.

phrases.translation: and act so viciously when you attack ˹others˺
phrases.explanation: The third charge is about violence. And act so viciously when you attack others, and the commentary explains this as their using force by killing with the sword and striking with whips whenever they seized anyone. The verse moves from vanity to cruelty, which is where pride in strength always ends. A people who believe they will live forever have no reason to restrain themselves against those who will not, and the buildings and the beatings are revealed as two expressions of the same arrogance.

phrases.translation: So fear Allah, and obey me
phrases.explanation: The call returns in the middle of the reproof. So fear Allah, and obey me, and the commentary explains this as the command to obey Allah in what He commands and forbids, and to stop the play and the amusement, the wronging of people, the domination by force, and the spreading of corruption in the land. The verse repeats the earlier call, but now it has content. After three charges, those words mean something specific, and obedience is asked for as the way out.

phrases.translation: Fear the One Who has provided you with ˹the good˺ things you know
phrases.explanation: Hud then turns from what they do to what they have been given. Fear the One Who has provided you with the good things you know, and the commentary explains this as warning them against the wrath of the One who gave them what they know from His side. The argument changes direction. Instead of only accusing them of cruelty, he names the gifts that made it possible, so that the strength they were proud of is a loan rather than a possession.

phrases.translation: He provided you with cattle, and children
phrases.explanation: The gifts are then listed. He provided you with cattle, and children, and the commentary explains this as Allah aiding them with livestock and with sons. These are the two measures of wealth and security in a pastoral people, and they are named first. The verse makes the case personal, since the herds in their valleys and the sons in their houses are things they could count, and every one of them came from the hand Hud is telling them to fear.

phrases.translation: and gardens, and springs
phrases.explanation: The list continues with gardens and water. And gardens, and springs, and the commentary explains these as the cultivated plots and the flowing rivers that sustained them. The pair completes the picture of a settled and prosperous people, with the produce of the earth and the water that made it grow. The verse is short because the reader can supply the rest, and because the point is not the inventory but who gave it.

phrases.translation: I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous day.”
phrases.explanation: The warning is then stated as a fear rather than a threat. I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous day, and the commentary explains this as his fear of the punishment of a mighty day from Allah. The word for fear is the same one used of Allah earlier, so the prophet's fear is now directed at their danger rather than at their power. He does not pronounce a sentence but says what he is afraid will happen to them.

phrases.translation: They responded, “It is all the same to us whether you warn ˹us˺ or not
phrases.explanation: Their answer is total indifference. It is all the same to us whether you warn us or not, they say, and the commentary explains this as their declaration that he may admonish them or hold back, since they will neither believe him nor accept what he brought. The reply does not dispute the charges about buildings or violence. It refuses to consider them, the most complete rejection a warner can receive, and it leaves the matter to be settled another way.

phrases.translation: This is simply the tradition of our predecessors
phrases.explanation: The people give their reason. This is simply the tradition of our predecessors, and the commentary records that reciters differ over one letter, reading it as the custom and religion of those before them or as their fabrication. It explains that either way the claim is the same, that what they do was handed down. Having refused the warning, they appeal to inheritance, as the people of Abraham did before them.

phrases.translation: And we will never be punished.”
phrases.explanation: The verse adds their conclusion. And we will never be punished, they say, and the commentary notes that this shows they did acknowledge a Creator while worshipping idols, in the manner of the Arab polytheists who said their gods brought them nearer to Allah. A people who expected no reckoning could do as they pleased. The whole dispute turns on that sentence, since if there is no punishment then the buildings, the violence, and the refusal cost nothing, and the next verse answers it.

phrases.translation: So they rejected him, and ˹so˺ We destroyed them.
phrases.explanation: The outcome is stated without detail. So they rejected him, and so We destroyed them, and the commentary explains the first as the Ad giving the lie to Hud and the second as their destruction for that denial. There is no account of a wind or a waiting period, only the connection between the two clauses. A people who said they would never be punished are answered in a sentence.

phrases.translation: Surely in this is a sign. Yet most of them would not believe
phrases.explanation: The refrain is then applied to the present. Surely in this is a sign, yet most of them would not believe, and the commentary explains the sign as a lesson for the people of Mecca who deny what the Prophet brought, since the destruction of Ad for rejecting their messenger shows how Allah deals with denial. The verse turns the ruin of an old nation into a warning for the living. What happened to them is offered as information rather than as revenge.

phrases.translation: And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The verse closes the narrative with the familiar pair. Your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful, and the commentary explains the first as power in vengeance on His enemies and the second as mercy toward those who believe in Him. The description comes after a destruction, which is where it is hardest to hear. The Lord who ends a nation is the same Lord who is merciful to anyone in it who turns.

phrases.translation: The people of Thamûd rejected the messengers
phrases.explanation: A fifth people follows. The people of Thamud rejected the messengers, and the commentary explains this as Thamud's denial of Allah's messengers when their brother Salih called them to Him and warned them for obeying those who spread corruption in the land. Thamud were the people of the carved rock dwellings, already listed among the destroyed. Their story opens in the same words as the others, so the pattern is heard before the difference.

phrases.translation: when their brother Ṣâliḥ said to them, “Will you not fear ˹Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The appeal is the same as before. When their brother Salih said to them, will you not fear Allah, and the commentary explains the question as asking whether they would not fear His punishment for their disobedience. The words are identical to those of Noah and Hud, which shows that the message does not change with the messenger. A new nation, a new prophet, and the same opening question, asked again because the answer had not changed.

phrases.translation: I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you
phrases.explanation: Salih states his standing. I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you, and the commentary explains this as his being sent by Allah to warn them of punishment when they transgress His command, and as a faithful custodian of the message entrusted to him for them. The claim is about the delivery and not the man. In each narrative the messenger begins by asking to be trusted with the words he carries, because everything else depends on whether the hearers think he invented them.

phrases.translation: So fear Allah, and obey me
phrases.explanation: Salih repeats the call. So fear Allah, and obey me, and the commentary explains this as the command to fear His punishment for disobedience and to obey Salih in his warning and in the command to follow Allah, so that they might be rightly guided. The two commands have already been heard twice in this chapter, and the repetition is not padding but testimony. Each prophet says the same thing, which is the argument that the message is one.

phrases.translation: I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺.
phrases.explanation: He then disowns any payment. I do not ask you for any reward for this message, and the commentary explains this as his seeking no recompense or wage for his sincere counsel and his warning. The third prophet to say this makes it a settled feature of the office. Whatever the people of Thamud might suspect about his motives, the verse removes the possibility that he is working for a share of the wealth their gardens produce.

phrases.translation: My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The verse names where his wage rests. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds, and the commentary explains this as his recompense resting with the Lord of everything in the heavens and the earth and all that is between them. The phrase widens the frame at exactly the point where the hearers are thinking about their own fields and flocks. A man paid by the Lord of all worlds cannot be hired by the people of one valley.

phrases.translation: Do you think you will be ˹forever˺ left secure in what you have here
phrases.explanation: Salih then turns to their sense of safety. Do you think you will be forever left secure in what you have here, and the commentary explains this as asking whether their Lord would leave them in this world in security with nothing to fear. The question is not about their wealth but about their assumption that it guarantees them. They lived among rocks they had hollowed out and gardens they had planted, and the verse asks what any of it would avail.

phrases.translation: amid gardens and springs
phrases.explanation: The first part of what they had is named. Amid gardens and springs, and the commentary explains these as orchards and flowing water. The words are plain because the hearers knew every tree and channel in them. The verse begins an inventory that will run to the palms and the carved houses, so that the reader feels how much was at stake and how little it counted in the end.

phrases.translation: and ˹various˺ crops, and palm trees ˹loaded˺ with tender fruit
phrases.explanation: The inventory continues with crops and palms. And various crops, and palm trees loaded with tender fruit, and the commentary explains the fruit as date clusters in their spathes, with reciters and exegetes differing over whether the final word means ripe and fully formed or broken and fallen. Either sense keeps the picture of abundance. The detail is agricultural and local, which is what makes the question about security so pointed.

phrases.translation: to carve homes in the mountains with great skill
phrases.explanation: The last item is their craftsmanship in stone. To carve homes in the mountains with great skill, and the commentary records two readings of the final word, one meaning skilled in carving and the other insolent and exultant. The two senses belong together, since the skill was real and the pride it fed was the problem. A people who could hollow a mountain into a house believed they had made themselves permanent, and their finest work stands as evidence against them.

phrases.translation: So fear Allah, and obey me
phrases.explanation: The call returns after the inventory. So fear Allah, and obey me, and the commentary explains this again as fearing His punishment for disobedience and obeying Salih in his counsel and warning. The repetition now carries the weight of everything just listed. He is not asking them to give up their gardens and their carved houses but to fear the One who gave them, and the verse places the demand directly after the reminder of what they would lose by refusing.

phrases.translation: And do not follow the command of the transgressors
phrases.explanation: The warning takes a political form. And do not follow the command of the transgressors, and the commentary explains this as Salih telling his people not to obey those who sin excessively against themselves by persisting in disobedience and daring to provoke Allah's wrath. The verse identifies a group rather than a practice. A whole community is being told that its direction is set by particular men, which means the refusal was never as general as it looked.

phrases.translation: who spread corruption throughout the land, never setting things right.”
phrases.explanation: The verse describes that group. Who spread corruption throughout the land, never setting things right, and the commentary identifies them as the nine men of Thamud who spread corruption and did no good, the same men described elsewhere as a group in the city who corrupted and did not reform. The word for setting right is the direct opposite of the corruption named first. Their offence was not only what they broke but their refusal to repair anything.

phrases.translation: They replied, “You are simply bewitched
phrases.explanation: The reply is an insult rather than an answer. You are simply bewitched, they say, and the commentary records that this means he was one of the bewitched, with one report adding the sense that he had been charmed or deluded. They do not engage with the warning about the corrupt leaders. Instead they explain away the man delivering it, which is the same move Pharaoh made and the same one the Meccans were making against the Prophet.

phrases.translation: You are only a human being like us,
phrases.explanation: The complaint is then spelled out. You are only a human being like us, and the commentary explains this as their saying that Salih ate what they ate and drank what they drank, and was neither a lord nor an angel, so why should they follow him. The objection is about the vessel rather than the message. A prophet drawn from the same town and the same meals was, in their eyes, too ordinary to be carrying anything extraordinary.

phrases.translation: so bring forth a sign if what you say is true.”
phrases.explanation: The demand follows. So bring forth a sign if what you say is true, and the commentary explains this as a request for a proof and indication that he was right, in the way a challenged man is asked to produce his evidence. The verse shows a people who will not weigh the message on its own terms but want a performance first. The sign is granted, which turns out to be the last mercy they receive.

phrases.translation: Ṣâliḥ said, “Here is a camel. She will have her turn to drink
phrases.explanation: Salih answers with the sign and its terms. Here is a camel, he says, and the commentary explains that he brought it forth from a rock at their demand. The wonder is not a display but a creature with claims on their water. The verse immediately sets out her share, taking the miracle out of the realm of spectacle and placing it in the ordinary economy of a desert town, where water is the thing people fight over.

phrases.translation: as you have yours, each on an appointed day
phrases.explanation: The arrangement is then stated precisely. Each on an appointed day, and the commentary explains the word as the share and portion of the water, so that neither she nor they may take from the other's day. The sign comes with a rule attached, and the rule is fair and testable. What they are asked to accept is not a mystery but a schedule, which makes their next move a plain decision about whether to keep their word.

phrases.translation: And do not ever touch her with harm,
phrases.explanation: The warning is added to the rule. And do not ever touch her with harm, and the commentary explains this as not harming her in any way, whether by cutting off her legs or killing her. The prohibition is absolute and the object is a single animal. A test that costs them nothing but a share of water is placed before them, and the verse makes clear that the consequence would fall on the whole community.

phrases.translation: or you will be overtaken by the torment of a tremendous day.”
phrases.explanation: The consequence is named. Or you will be overtaken by the torment of a tremendous day, and the commentary explains this as the punishment of a day whose punishment is tremendous descending on them from Allah. The wording does not say when, only that it will overtake them. They had asked for a sign to prove the messenger true, and the sign arrived with a condition, so that the proof and the test are the same event.

phrases.translation: But they killed her, becoming regretful
phrases.explanation: The verse records what they did with the test. But they killed her, becoming regretful, and the commentary explains that Thamud transgressed their prophet's command and hamstrung the she-camel, and that they regretted it afterwards, though the regret availed them nothing. The killing is attributed to the group, as the warning had been. A single act by a few men brought a whole nation under a sentence, and the verse notes the regret precisely because it came too late to be repentance.

phrases.translation: So the punishment overtook them.
phrases.explanation: The sentence falls as promised. So the punishment overtook them, and the commentary explains this as the punishment Salih had announced striking them and destroying them. Nothing is said about how it came, because the chapter is tracking the pattern rather than the weather. The warning had been specific, the transgression had been specific, and the verse simply records that the two met, which is what makes it a sign for anyone willing to read it.

phrases.translation: Surely in this is a sign. Yet most of them would not believe
phrases.explanation: The refrain follows. Surely in this is a sign, yet most of them would not believe, and the commentary explains the sign as the destruction of Thamud for hamstringing the camel and transgressing the prophet's command, a lesson for whoever takes one, and it adds that most of them would not believe according to Allah's knowledge. The verse addresses the Meccans who had just been told the story. The evidence is not lacking, only the willingness to be persuaded.

phrases.translation: And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The verse closes the Thamud account. Your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful, and the commentary explains the first as His vengeance on His enemies and the second as His mercy toward those of His creatures who believe in Him. The two names are the chapter's steady refrain, appearing after every destruction. They keep the reader from hearing these stories as mere history of cruelty, since each one ends with a description of the Lord who is both severe and kind.

phrases.translation: The people of Lot rejected the messengers
phrases.explanation: A sixth people is named. The people of Lot rejected the messengers, and the commentary explains this as their denial of those Allah had sent to them when they came. Lot's people are introduced in the same words as the others, though their sin was different. The chapter is making clear that the denial is what runs through all these nations, whatever particular form their corruption took, and that the same end follows the same refusal.

phrases.translation: when their brother Lot said to them, “Will you not fear ˹Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The appeal is again the same. When their brother Lot said to them, will you not fear Allah, and the commentary explains the question as his address to his people, asking whether they would not fear Him. Lot was a stranger among them in lineage, yet the Quran still calls him their brother, which ties him to the town he warned. The verse opens a story about a city whose sin was notorious, and it begins with the gentlest possible question.

phrases.translation: I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you
phrases.explanation: Lot states his standing as the others did. I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you, and the commentary explains this as his being a messenger from their Lord, trustworthy in safeguarding the revelation and in conveying the message. The claim is about custody of the words he carried. In a town where he was an outsider, the only thing he could ask them to judge was whether he had been faithful with what he had been given.

phrases.translation: So fear Allah, and obey me
phrases.explanation: The call is the familiar one. So fear Allah, and obey me, and the commentary explains the first as fearing His punishment for denying His messenger, and the second as obeying Lot in what he called them to, with the promise of guidance for those who did. The words are exactly those of Noah, Hud, and Salih. By now the repetition is a structure, so the reader hears the same offer made to a sixth people before the story turns.

phrases.translation: I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺.
phrases.explanation: Lot also refuses payment. I do not ask you for any reward for this message, and the commentary explains this as his seeking no recompense or wage for his counsel and his summoning them to his Lord. The verse removes the suspicion of a man who might be after the wealth of a prosperous town. Every messenger in this chapter has said it, and the repetition is the point, since a message that is sold is not a message but a transaction.

phrases.translation: My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The verse names where his wage rests. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds, and the commentary explains this as his reward for summoning them to Allah, for his counsel, and for conveying the messages resting solely with the Lord of the worlds. The phrase returns for the fourth time. What is being established across these narratives is a single standard of prophecy, one that has no price and no patron among the people being addressed.

phrases.translation: Why do you ˹men˺ lust after fellow men
phrases.explanation: Lot names the practice directly. Why do you lust after fellow men, and the commentary explains the question as asking whether they approached the males of the children of Adam in the way a man approaches a woman. The verse states the accusation without decoration and puts it as a question. It is asked by a man who lived among them and knew exactly what they did, and the form of a question leaves open the possibility that they might answer and turn.

phrases.translation: leaving the wives that your Lord has created for you?
phrases.explanation: The verse adds what they were leaving. Leaving the wives that your Lord has created for you, and the commentary explains this as forsaking what Allah had made lawful for them in their spouses. The argument is about what they refused as well as what they did, since the created order they disregarded stood in their own houses. The word created is deliberate, making the arrangement a matter of what Allah made rather than of local custom.

phrases.translation: In fact, you are a transgressing people.”
phrases.explanation: The verdict is then pronounced. In fact, you are a transgressing people, and the commentary explains the word as describing a people who go beyond the limit set for them. The sentence ends the speech and closes the conversation. Lot has already told them who he is and what he came with, and now he tells them what they have become, which leaves them with nothing to answer and the next verse shows how they answered anyway.

phrases.translation: They threatened, “If you do not desist, O Lot, you will surely be expelled.”
phrases.explanation: The reply is a threat of expulsion. They said that if he did not desist, O Lot, he would be among those driven out, and the commentary explains this as a warning that he would be expelled from their town and land if he kept forbidding them. The messenger is told to stop or leave. The demand is not that he join them but that he stop objecting, which is what the town did with Noah and Hud.

phrases.translation: Lot responded, “I am truly one of those who despise your ˹shameful˺ practice
phrases.explanation: Lot answers with loathing rather than argument. I am truly one of those who despise your practice, and the commentary explains this as his declaring that he abhors the deed they commit and rejects it utterly. The word places him among those who hate the thing, not merely those who avoid it. Having failed to persuade them, he states where he stands, and the statement is a separation, since a man cannot live in a town whose defining act he despises.

phrases.translation: My Lord! Save me and my family from ˹the consequences of˺ what they do.”
phrases.explanation: He then turns to his Lord. My Lord, save me and my family from the consequences of what they do, and the commentary explains this as the prayer he made after they threatened to expel him, asking to be delivered from the punishment that would fall on them. The prayer is about rescue rather than victory. Lot does not ask to be vindicated in the square but to be taken out of the way of what is coming.

phrases.translation: So We saved him and all of his family
phrases.explanation: The answer comes at once. So We saved him and all of his family, and the commentary explains this as delivering him and his household from the punishment with which the people of Lot were punished. The word all is important, because the exception that follows shows how narrowly it is meant. A man who had despaired of his town is given his household, and the rescue is described as a direct answer to the prayer of the previous verse.

phrases.translation: except an old woman, who was one of the doomed
phrases.explanation: The exception is then stated. Except an old woman, who was one of the doomed, and the commentary explains that this was Lot's wife, destroyed with the household because she used to inform her people about the guests. It records a view that she left with Lot and was struck by the stones afterwards. The verse keeps mercy and judgement in one sentence, since the household was saved and one of its members was not.

phrases.translation: Then We utterly destroyed the rest
phrases.explanation: The verse records the end of the town. Then We utterly destroyed the rest, and the commentary explains this as the destruction of the remainder of Lot's people. The word utterly is chosen because nothing of them remained. The household had just been taken out, and the sentence falls on everyone else, which makes the two verses read as one action with two outcomes. The town that threatened expulsion is removed, and the man it wanted to drive out survives it.

phrases.translation: pouring upon them a rain ˹of brimstone˺.
phrases.explanation: The manner of the destruction is then described. Pouring upon them a rain of brimstone, and the commentary explains this as Allah sending down upon them stones of baked clay from the sky. The punishment matches the sin in the way this chapter's punishments always do, since a people who pursued what was not theirs were covered by what fell from above. The image is of a sky that turns against them rather than of an army at the gate.

phrases.translation: How evil was the rain of those who had been warned
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with a judgement on that rain. How evil was the rain of those who had been warned, and the commentary explains this as asking how wretched that rain was, the rain of a people who had been warned by their prophet and had denied him. The warning is named in the same breath as the punishment, which is the point. What fell on them was not an unexplained disaster but the answer to a message they had heard and rejected.

phrases.translation: Surely in this is a sign. Yet most of them would not believe
phrases.explanation: The refrain closes the Lot narrative. Surely in this is a sign, and the commentary explains the sign as the destruction of Lot's people for denying their messenger, a lesson for the Prophet's own people so that they might take heed about their own denial. It adds that most of them were not believers in Allah's prior knowledge. The verse ties the ruined town to Mecca, since the same warning had been delivered in both places and the same refusal had followed it.

phrases.translation: And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The verse names the pair once more. Your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful, and the commentary explains the mercy as directed toward whoever believes in Him, while the power is shown in what happened to those who did not. The order matters, since the mercy is named last. After a rain of stones, the chapter insists on ending with the attribute that leaves a way open, because the next narrative begins with a new people who still had time to hear.

phrases.translation: The residents of the Forest rejected the messengers
phrases.explanation: A seventh people is introduced. The residents of the Forest rejected the messengers, and the commentary explains the forest as densely growing trees, with reports identifying these dwellers as the people of Madyan. The name describes a place rather than a tribe, which is fitting for a people known by their trees and their trade. The story opens in the familiar words, and the reader already knows what the ending of such a sentence has been in every case so far.

phrases.translation: when Shu’aib said to them, “Will you not fear ˹Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The appeal is unchanged. When Shuayb said to them, will you not fear Allah, and the commentary explains the question as his asking whether they would not fear His punishment for disobedience to their Lord. The seventh messenger asks the seventh time, and the formula has become almost liturgical. What changes between the narratives is not the message but the particular shape of each people's corruption, and the next verses will show what Madyan's was.

phrases.translation: I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you
phrases.explanation: Shuayb states his standing. I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you, and the commentary explains this as his being a messenger from Allah, trustworthy in preserving His revelation. The claim is the same as in every previous account, and by now the reader understands its function. Before a prophet names a fault, he establishes that he is not inventing the accusation, since everything depends on whether the words are his or the One who sent him.

phrases.translation: So fear Allah, and obey me
phrases.explanation: The call is repeated for the last time in these narratives. So fear Allah, and obey me, and the commentary explains this briefly as fearing His punishment for opposing His command and obeying Shuayb so that they might be rightly guided. The formula has now been spoken by seven messengers. What makes this one different is what follows it, since the next verses name specific commercial practices rather than the general corruption of a proud nation.

phrases.translation: I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺.
phrases.explanation: Shuayb disowns any payment. I do not ask you for any reward for this message, and the commentary explains this as his seeking no recompense for his sincere counsel. The phrasing is identical to the other narratives, but in a town of traders the point is sharper, since the man speaking is refusing the very thing his hearers would have assumed he wanted. A messenger who wants no money cannot be bought, and cannot be accused of preaching for profit.

phrases.translation: My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The verse states where his wage rests. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds, and the commentary explains this as his reward and recompense resting with the Lord of the worlds alone. Then the same verse moves directly into the command to give full measure, with no pause between the two. The transition is deliberate, since the one who is not cheating them for gain is the one entitled to tell them not to cheat others.

phrases.translation: Give full measure, and cause no loss ˹to others˺
phrases.explanation: The first charge concerns the measure. Give full measure, and cause no loss to others, and the commentary explains this as giving people their rights in full when measuring and not being among those who shortchange them. The command is not an abstraction but a rule about the scale in the market. In a trading town the first test of honesty is the instrument in the hand, and the verse begins there rather than with belief.

phrases.translation: Weigh with an even balance
phrases.explanation: The same demand is then put in another form. Weigh with an even balance, and the commentary explains the balance as the straight scale in which there is no shortfall for the one being weighed for. The repetition with a different instrument shows that the command covers every means of measuring, so that no trader could keep one honest scale for show and another for use. The verse is short and exact, and its brevity suits a rule meant to be applied daily.

phrases.translation: and do not defraud people of their property.
phrases.explanation: The charge widens from instruments to property. And do not defraud people of their property, and the commentary explains this as not shortchanging people in their rights when measuring and weighing. The word covers any taking of what is not owed, so that the command is no longer only about weights but about the whole conduct of trade. The verse treats the scale as one example of a habit, and it names the habit before naming the wider harm.

phrases.translation: Nor go about spreading corruption in the land
phrases.explanation: The second half turns to the land. Nor go about spreading corruption in the land, and the commentary explains this as not spreading corruption in abundance on the earth. The two clauses together show how a market town decays, first by small dishonesties in the scale and then by a general disorder that follows from them. Shuayb is not accusing them of idolatry here but of the daily practices that make a community unable to trust itself.

phrases.translation: And fear the One Who created you and ˹all˺ earlier peoples.”
phrases.explanation: The speech ends with a reminder of origin. And fear the One Who created you and all earlier peoples, and the commentary explains this as fearing the punishment of the Lord who created them and the generations before them. The verse widens the frame from the market to the whole history of the town. Their ancestors were created by the same hand, which means the practices they inherited carry no authority against the One who made both them and their fathers.

phrases.translation: They replied, “You are simply bewitched
phrases.explanation: The reply is the same insult heard in Thamud. They said, you are simply bewitched, and the commentary explains this as their saying that he was only a man afflicted by the need for food and drink as they were, and not an angel. The answer dodges the charges about the scale entirely. Rather than deny that they shortchange their customers, they question the sanity of the man who mentioned it, which has been the response of every guilty party in this chapter.

phrases.translation: Also, you are only a human being like us,
phrases.explanation: The second objection is about his humanity. Also, you are only a human being like us, they say, and the commentary explains this as their pointing out that he eats and drinks as they do. The argument is that a messenger should be made of something other than the people he is sent to, which would make the message a spectacle rather than a summons. The verse shows a town willing to accept almost anything except a neighbour with a claim on them.

phrases.translation: and we think you are indeed a liar
phrases.explanation: The verse then adds the accusation. And we think you are indeed a liar, and the commentary explains this as their regarding him as someone who lies in what he tells them and in what he invites them to. Having failed to answer the charges about the scale, they deny that he tells the truth at all, without saying which part is false. The insult is broad because the alternative would be to examine the claims, and that is what they will not do.

phrases.translation: So cause ˹deadly˺ pieces of the sky to fall upon
phrases.explanation: They then set their own test. So cause deadly pieces of the sky to fall upon us, they say, and the commentary explains the pieces as fragments of the sky, a plural of the word for a piece. The demand is for a sign of the kind that would settle the matter by force. They do not ask for evidence they could weigh but for a destruction they could watch, which is a challenge issued by people who do not expect it to be accepted.

phrases.translation: us, if what you say is true.”
phrases.explanation: The condition is added. If what you say is true, they say, and the verse ends there, leaving the challenge hanging in the air. The phrase is the same one used by Thamud and by Pharaoh before them, and in each case the sign came. The verse shows the exact form of unbelief in this town, a demand that God prove Himself on command, and the next verses record an answer that was not the one they were expecting.

phrases.translation: Shu’aib responded, “My Lord knows best whatever you do.”
phrases.explanation: Shuayb does not accept their terms. My Lord knows best whatever you do, he answers, and the commentary explains this as his saying that Allah is fully aware of their deeds, that nothing of them is hidden from Him, and that He will repay them as is due. The reply hands the matter over rather than arguing further. He does not call down the sky and does not defend himself, since the One who sees everything needs no briefing from a prophet under pressure.

phrases.translation: So they rejected him, and ˹so˺ were overtaken by the torment of the day of the ˹deadly˺ cloud.
phrases.explanation: The answer came anyway. So they rejected him, and so were overtaken by the torment of the day of the deadly cloud, and the commentary explains this as a cloud overshadowing them, so that when they had gathered beneath it, it blazed over them into fire and burned them. It records that a heat had struck them first, driving them out, and that they went to the cloud for relief. The sign they demanded arrived as the thing they had asked for.

phrases.translation: That was really a torment of a tremendous day
phrases.explanation: The verse then judges that day. That was really a torment of a tremendous day, and the commentary keeps the weight on the word torment, which is doubled in the sentence for emphasis. The cloud looked like shade and turned out to be fire, which is the pattern of a town that called its own honesty into question and then called down the sky. The verse ends the narrative without a single word of comfort for the people who asked for it.

phrases.translation: Surely in this is a sign. Yet most of them would not believe
phrases.explanation: The refrain closes the seventh story. Surely in this is a sign, and the commentary explains the sign as the punishment of the people of Shuayb by the day of the cloud because they denied their prophet, a lesson for the Prophet's own people that Allah's way with those who deny is the same now as it was then. Yet most of them would not believe. The verse names the pattern one final time before the chapter turns from the messengers to the book itself.

phrases.translation: And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The verse names the pair for the last time in this series. Your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful, and the commentary explains the first as power in punishing those of His enemies whom He punishes, and the second as mercy toward those of His creatures who repent and return to obedience. The refrain has followed every destroyed nation from Noah to Shuayb. After seven such endings, the reader has been taught to expect both names together, and the chapter relies on that expectation.

phrases.translation: This is certainly a revelation from the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The subject shifts from prophets to the book. This is certainly a revelation from the Lord of all worlds, and the commentary explains this as the Quran itself being sent down from the Lord of the worlds, with the pronoun referring back to the reminder mentioned earlier in the chapter. After seven narratives of messengers rejected, the verse states what the Prophet carries. The stories were never the point, only the record of what happens to those who reject the like of what he brought.

phrases.translation: which the trustworthy spirit ˹Gabriel˺ brought down
phrases.explanation: The verse names who carried the revelation. Which the trustworthy spirit brought down, and the commentary explains the spirit as Gabriel, noting that reciters differ over the verb and over whether the spirit is the subject or the object, and accepting both readings as close in meaning. Either way the book has a carrier and a source. The Quran is not a text that appeared among people but something conveyed by a trusted agent of the Lord of all worlds.

phrases.translation: into your heart ˹O Prophet˺—so that you may be one of the warners—
phrases.explanation: The verse names the place it reached. Into your heart, so that you may be one of the warners, and the commentary explains this as the spirit reciting it to the Prophet until he had memorized it in his heart, and as his being placed among the messengers who warned their peoples. The heart rather than a page is named, which matters for a man who had to recite under pressure. What he carried was not a document he could lose.

phrases.translation: in a clear Arabic tongue
phrases.explanation: The language of that revelation is then stated. In a clear Arabic tongue, and the commentary explains this as sent down in the tongue of the Arabs so that its meaning would be plain to whoever heard it. It adds that the reason is to remove the excuse of the Quraysh, who might otherwise say that it came in a language they did not know. The verse closes the door on that objection while leaving every other one for the next verses to answer.

phrases.translation: And it has indeed been ˹foretold˺ in the Scriptures of those before
phrases.explanation: The book is then placed in a longer history. And it has indeed been foretold in the Scriptures of those before, and the commentary explains this as its being mentioned in the books of earlier nations, noting that the general wording means that its mention occurs in some of the Books Allah sent down. The Quran is not announced as a novelty. It is presented as the fulfilment of what earlier communities had been told to expect.

phrases.translation: Was it not sufficient proof for the deniers that it has been recognized by the knowledgeable among the Children of Israel
phrases.explanation: A proof is then drawn from the experts. Was it not sufficient proof for the deniers that it has been recognized by the knowledgeable among the Children of Israel, and the commentary explains this as asking whether it is not evidence that the truth of the book is known to their scholars, with reports naming Abdullah ibn Salam. The argument is from informed testimony. Those who knew the earlier books best saw in this one what those books described.

phrases.translation: Had We revealed it to a non-Arab
phrases.explanation: A hypothetical case is then put. Had We revealed it to a non-Arab, and the commentary explains the word as one whose speech is indistinct, meaning someone who does not speak eloquent Arabic, whether he was from the Arabs or from outside them. The point is ability rather than ethnicity. The verse sets messenger against message, since an Arabic book delivered by a man who could not speak Arabic would prove nothing.

phrases.translation: who would then recite it to the deniers ˹in fluent Arabic˺, still they would not have believed in it
phrases.explanation: The case is completed. Who would then recite it to the deniers in fluent Arabic, still they would not have believed in it, and the commentary records that one of the Companions, standing at Arafah, said that even if it had come down on his camel and the camel had spoken it, they would not have believed. The obstacle was never the tongue but the refusal of the hearers.

phrases.translation: This is how We allow denial ˹to steep˺ into the hearts of the wicked
phrases.explanation: The verse explains how the refusal became settled. This is how We allow denial to steep into the hearts of the wicked, and the commentary explains the verb as Allah threading or inserting the denial into their hearts, with reports describing it as unbelief or as the associating of partners with Allah. The image is of something poured in and absorbed. Having described a people who would not believe even if a camel spoke Arabic, it names a heart that has stopped receiving.

phrases.translation: They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment
phrases.explanation: The result of that condition is then stated. They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment, and the commentary explains this as their not holding the Quran to be true until the punishment comes upon them in this life, like the communities whose stories the chapter has told. Belief at that point is not belief but the recognition of a fact. The verse marks the boundary of the argument, since a case that has been answered can still be refused.

phrases.translation: which will take them by surprise when they least expect ˹it˺
phrases.explanation: The timing of that arrival is then described. Which will take them by surprise when they least expect it, and the commentary explains this as the punishment coming upon them suddenly, without their having any prior knowledge of it until it overtakes them. The verse adds a quality that the earlier narratives did not stress. A people who had demanded a sign on their own schedule are told that the thing they were challenging will not announce itself.

phrases.translation: Then they will cry, “Can we be allowed more time?”
phrases.explanation: Their response at that moment is quoted. Then they will cry, can we be allowed more time, and the commentary explains this as their asking whether the punishment might be lifted and their lives extended so that they could repent and turn from their disbelief to faith and obedience. It is the same wish the people of the fire expressed in the earlier passage. Having spent a life refusing, they ask for one more moment, and the next verse answers with a question.

phrases.translation: Do they ˹really˺ seek to hasten Our torment
phrases.explanation: The verse turns the demand back on them. Do they really seek to hasten Our torment, and the commentary explains this as addressed to the polytheists who had challenged the Prophet to bring down fragments of the sky. The word for hasten is exact, since they had asked for the punishment to be hurried. The verse points out the contradiction. The same people who now beg for delay had demanded that judgement arrive immediately, and the question exposes how little they thought it through.

phrases.translation: Imagine ˹O Prophet˺ if We allowed them enjoyment for years
phrases.explanation: A hypothetical is then offered. Imagine if We allowed them enjoyment for years, and the commentary places this beside the verses about the punishment overtaking them suddenly, as the alternative that was actually granted them. The verse asks the reader to consider a long stretch of comfort. Time is the mercy that was given, and the question is what they did with it. The next verse shows that a delay is not a reprieve, since the thing promised still arrives at the end of it.

phrases.translation: then there came to them what they had been threatened with
phrases.explanation: The hypothetical ends where every life ends. Then there came to them what they had been threatened with, and the commentary explains this as the punishment befalling them as promised for their disbelief in the signs and their denial of the messenger. The verse does not say how many years passed, because their number is not the point. What was delayed arrived, and everything the years contained was cancelled by it, which is the answer to anyone who mistakes a delay for a verdict.

phrases.translation: would that enjoyment be of any benefit to them ˹at all˺
phrases.explanation: The verse answers the previous hypothetical. Would that enjoyment be of any benefit to them at all, and the commentary explains this as asking what the long life and the comfort availed them now that they never repented, and adds that it did not help but harmed them, since they added sins and gathered transgressions they would not have gathered without it. The question removes the last comfort from people given time. Years of ease are a heavier account, not a lighter one.

phrases.translation: We have never destroyed a society without warners
phrases.explanation: The chapter then states a principle. We have never destroyed a society without warners, and the commentary explains this as referring to the settlements described in this surah, which were only destroyed after messengers had come to them warning of punishment for their disbelief. The verse answers any suggestion that the peoples of the earlier narratives were caught without notice. Every town destroyed in this chapter had a messenger in it first, which is why the pattern was never arbitrary.

phrases.translation: to remind ˹them˺, for We would never wrong ˹anyone˺
phrases.explanation: The purpose of those messengers is then given, and so is the justice of the outcome. To remind them, for We would never wrong anyone, and the commentary explains this as the warning being a reminder and an admonition, and as Allah not being unjust in punishing and destroying them, since He did so only after they rebelled, were ungrateful, and worshipped others, and only after the proof had been established and the warnings delivered. The verse places every destruction under one claim about fairness.

phrases.translation: It was not the devils who brought this ˹Quran˺ down
phrases.explanation: A denial is then answered directly. It was not the devils who brought this Quran down, and the commentary explains this as saying that the devils did not descend with it upon Muhammad, but rather the trustworthy spirit descends with it upon him. The charge answered is that revelation came from an unclean source, a common accusation against a man reciting what no one could match. The verse names the carrier, and the next verses explain what the devils actually do.

phrases.translation: it is not for them ˹to do so˺, nor can they
phrases.explanation: The verse states two reasons at once. It is not for them to do so, nor can they, and the commentary explains the first as saying it does not befit the devils to descend with the Quran, and the second as saying they are unable to do it. The distinction is between worthiness and capacity. They would not be the right carriers even if they could, and they could not even if the task were given, which closes the accusation from both sides.

phrases.translation: for they are strictly barred from ˹even˺ overhearing ˹it˺
phrases.explanation: The verse explains why they cannot. For they are strictly barred from even overhearing it, and the commentary explains this as the devils being cut off from listening to the Quran where it is in the heaven, and asks how they could then bring it down. The image is of a guarded place and excluded listeners. Having answered the charge that revelation came from an unclean source, the verse shows the source is not merely wrong for them but sealed against them.

phrases.translation: So do not ever call upon any other god besides Allah,
phrases.explanation: The address turns to the Prophet himself. So do not ever call upon any other god besides Allah, and the commentary explains this as the command not to worship any deity alongside Him. The verse is directed to the messenger, which is striking after so much condemnation of the polytheists. It places him under the same obligation he is preaching, so that the warning is not a message he delivers from outside but a rule that binds him first.

phrases.translation: or you will be one of the punished
phrases.explanation: The consequence is then stated. Or you will be one of the punished, and the commentary explains this as the warning that punishment would descend on him just as it descended on those who transgressed the command and worshipped others. The words are addressed to the most honoured of creatures, which makes them a statement about the command rather than about his character. No station exempts anyone from the first obligation, and the verse secures that point at the very end of the chapter.

phrases.translation: And warn ˹all, starting with˺ your closest relatives
phrases.explanation: The command then narrows to those nearest him. And warn all, starting with your closest relatives, and the commentary explains this as the command to warn his nearest kinsfolk and frighten them with the punishment. It records that when the verse came down he began with the sons of Abd al-Muttalib and his own household, calling on Safiyya and Fatima and telling them he could avail them nothing against Allah. A universal message begins at home.

phrases.translation: and be gracious to the believers who follow you
phrases.explanation: The verse then turns to the believers. And be gracious to the believers who follow you, and the commentary explains the phrase as gentleness in dealing and in speech toward those who followed him. One report says that when the earlier verse came down and he began with his household, the Muslims felt it heavily, and this verse was revealed. The same man is told to warn his family without softening and to be gentle with those who accepted.

phrases.translation: But if they disobey you, say, “I am certainly free of what you do.”
phrases.explanation: The verse provides for the refusal of his own family. But if they disobey you, say, I am certainly free of what you do, and the commentary explains this as what he was told to say to his near kinsfolk if they clung to idol worship and to ascribing partners to the All-Merciful. The word free declares distance, not hatred. A man cannot carry his relatives into belief, and the verse gives him what to say when the warning has been delivered and refused.

phrases.translation: Put your trust in the Almighty, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The next command turns him toward reliance. Put your trust in the Almighty, Most Merciful, and the commentary explains the first name as the ground of confidence in His vengeance upon His enemies, and the second as mercy toward whoever turns back and repents. The two names answer the situation of the previous verse. Told that his own family might refuse, he is told where to place his weight, and the One trusted can avenge and forgive.

phrases.translation: Who sees you when you rise ˹for prayer at night˺
phrases.explanation: The verse then names what that trust rests on. Who sees you when you rise for prayer at night, and the commentary explains this as the One who sees him when he stands for prayer, with one report giving the sense wherever he may be. The night prayer is named because it is the act no one sees. A servant who is watched in the dark is not working for an audience, and the verse makes the unseen vigil the place where sincerity is measured.

phrases.translation: as well as your movements ˹in prayer˺ along with ˹fellow˺ worshippers
phrases.explanation: The verse extends the seeing to his movements. As well as your movements in prayer along with fellow worshippers, and the commentary records the view that this means his standing, bowing, and prostrating in the prayer, and another that it means his movements among those who pray behind him. Either reading turns the physical sequence of the ritual into something observed. The One who sees him stand also sees him bend and fall, and the whole of the prayer is placed within His sight.

phrases.translation: He ˹alone˺ is indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing
phrases.explanation: The verse names the two attributes behind that seeing. He alone is indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing, and the commentary explains the first as Allah hearing his recitation and remembrance in the prayer, and the second as knowing what he performs in it and what the one praying with him performs. The pair matches the earlier verse, hearing what is said and knowing what is meant. The verse closes by telling him that nothing in the prayer, neither words nor movements, is hidden.

phrases.translation: Shall I inform you of whom the devils ˹actually˺ descend upon
phrases.explanation: The chapter returns to the accusation about the source of revelation. Shall I inform you of whom the devils actually descend upon, and the commentary explains the question as addressed to people and answered in the next verse. The verse is a challenge, inviting the hearers to compare two kinds of inspiration. Having denied that devils brought the Quran, it now says who the devils do visit, leaving the hearers to see which description fits whom.

phrases.translation: They descend upon every sinful liar
phrases.explanation: The answer is given at once. They descend upon every sinful liar, and the commentary explains the phrase as every great liar and slanderer among people, and records that the soothsayers were meant, since the jinn would steal a hearing and bring it to their allies among people. The verse describes a transaction between a hidden source and a dishonest recipient. A message that arrives in secret and is repeated as a lie belongs to this category, and the Quran is placed firmly outside it.

phrases.translation: who gives an ˹attentive˺ ear ˹to half-truths˺, mostly passing on sheer lies
phrases.explanation: The verse describes how that transaction works. Who gives an attentive ear to half-truths, mostly passing on sheer lies, and the commentary explains this as the devils casting down what they had heard upon every great liar, and as most of those who receive it lying in what they report. The picture is of information overheard and then corrupted in the telling. It is a precise account of soothsaying, and it shows why such a channel could never produce a book that survives scrutiny.

phrases.translation: As for poets, they are followed ˹merely˺ by deviants
phrases.explanation: The chapter turns to the poets. As for poets, they are followed merely by deviants, and the commentary explains this as saying the erring follow them and not the rightly guided, with views that the deviants are those who transmit their poetry or the devils. The verse answers another accusation, that the Prophet was a poet. It does not condemn poetry but distinguishes a messenger, followed by people seeking guidance, from a poet followed by people seeking amusement.

phrases.translation: Do you not see how they rant in every field
phrases.explanation: The verse describes the poets' method. Do you not see how they rant in every field, and the commentary explains this as their plunging into every folly, or ranging through every branch of poetry, or simply speaking in every direction. The image is of water spreading where there is no channel. A poet may praise and blame the same person, argue both sides, and never be held to a conclusion, which is the opposite of a message that must be lived.

phrases.translation: only saying what they never do
phrases.explanation: The verse names the gap between their words and their lives. Only saying what they never do, and the commentary records a report in which a man asked about these verses and was told they concern the poets of the polytheists, not the poets of the believers, with the exception that follows making the point. The charge is not that poetry is false but that it costs nothing. One who praises courage and flees the field has told a truth and lived a lie.

phrases.translation: Except those who believe, do good, remember Allah often, and ˹poetically˺ avenge ˹the believers˺ after being wrongfully slandered.
phrases.explanation: The exception is then stated. Except those who believe, do good, remember Allah often, and poetically avenge the believers after being wrongfully slandered, and the commentary explains that this was revealed concerning the poets of the Messenger, such as Hassan ibn Thabit and Kab ibn Malik, and that it applies to everyone with that quality. The four conditions cover belief, conduct, remembrance, and verse used in defence of the community. Poetry is not condemned but held to the same obligations.

phrases.translation: The wrongdoers will come to know what ˹evil˺ end they will meet
phrases.explanation: The chapter ends with a warning. The wrongdoers will come to know what evil end they will meet, and the commentary explains this as the closing statement of the surah after the exception. The verse returns to the note struck throughout, from the first complaint about those who would not believe to the seven ruined nations. The book has been vindicated, the messenger defended, and the hearers left with a sentence that applies to them as much as to anyone in the stories.
